THE Harris Foundation Lectures at the University of Chicago have been made possible through the generosity of the heirs of Norman Wait Harris and Emma Gale Harris, who donated to the University a fund to be known as 'The Norman Wait Harris Memorial Foundation" on January 27, 1923. The letter of gift contains the following statement: It is apparent that a knowledge of world-affairs was never of more importance to Americans than today. The spirit of distrust which pervades the Old World is not without its effect upon our own country. How to combat this disintegrating tendency is a problem worthy of the most serious thought. Perhaps one of the best methods is the promotion of a better understanding of other nations through wisely directed educational effort. The purpose of the foundation shall be the promotion of a better understanding on the part of American citizens of the other peoples of the world, thus establishing a basis for improved international relations and a more enlightened world-order. The aim shall always be to give accurate information, not to propagate opinion. Annual Institutes have been held at the University of Chicago since the summer of 1924. This series of volumes includes the lectures there delivered, in essentially their original form.

The First and Second Institutes on the Harris Foundation dealt respectively with European and Far Eastern affairs. The Third Institute, in the summer of 1926, has been devoted to the problems of Mexico. This volume, entitled Aspects of Mexican Civilization, contains the lectures of Honorable José Vasconcelos, former Secretary of Education of Mexico, and Honorable Manuel Gamio, former Director of the Bureau of Anthropology and Sub-Secretary of the Department of Education of Mexico. A second volume, Some Mexican Problems, contains the lectures of Honorable Moises Saenz, Sub-Secretary of the Department of Education of Mexico, and Professor Herbert I. Priestley, of the History Department of the University of California and author of The Mexican Nation, a History.

Many travelers have recorded the same impression; even casual observers have seen that Mexico's most striking feature is the extreme difference in the appearance of the inhabitants, in the nature of the soil, in the climate of nearby sections, abyssmal differences in the thought of the people and in the landscape of the country. Perhaps there is no other nation on earth where you can find, in the same accentuated form, a coexistence of human types separated by centuries and even by epochs of ethnographical development—peopledifferentin blood, race tradition, and habits. And such plurality of types is not a new condition that might be attributed to the Spanish invasion alone, because long before the Spaniards landed, a mixture of peoples existed, and the Spaniards only contributed one more race-wave in the already mixed waters of our national plasma. Remember that archaeologists tell us there is no connecting link between the race that built the Teotihuacan pyramids and the Aztecs of the day of Montezuma. The Aztecs themselves were invaders and comparative newcomers

who had overwhelmed the Chichimecs, and then the Chichimec on his part, had received practically no inheritance, at least no direct influence, from the builders of the ancient palaces. Also there is no known relation between any of the successive civilizations of the plateau and the wonder-builders of the Maya-Quiché hot contries of Guatemala, Yucatan, and Tabasco-the race that has left such a magnificent testimony of its genius in the monuments whose silent messages have not yet been deciphered. All countries, you may say, all old countries, show the landmarks of this uninterrupted work of history through which races arise, prosper, and then decay only to be overpowered and replaced by newcomers; but the one fact I wish to emphasize is the fact that Mexico is a land where the process of history has been one of continuous destruction and substitution of cultures instead of the regular growing and evolving of one period into the other. With constantly alternated and disconnected efforts of enlightenment, instead of a continuous cumulative progression, the Mexico of today still shows trace of the multiplied experience of our history. Independent and even conflicting manners of culture have developed in our land and sometimes have become enrooted in it; but suddenly they are driven

away, or they disappear through decay, before they are able to evolve into a higher civilization; they are like a stem giving out a beautiful flower only to die without leaving a seed. And thus the soil remains barren until another accidental flora, independent of the preceding one, comes in turn to life. Instead of an evolutionary series of events, as you may find for instance in the history of Europe, the history of Mexico will show you a number of glorious but lonely, disconnected efforts like sparks in the darkness, and in the background a constantly recurring tragedy of destruction and anarchy. In this manner even the wise of every period find themselves unable to take advantages of the cultural conquests of the preceding epoch; and each new period through the destruction of the past finds itself in the need of building anew the whole fabric of social life. Such an overwhelming undertaking consumes, of course, the national energy and postpones the realization of truly transcendent plans. A series of layers composed of materials that do not mix-such is the sketch of our history. A compound of races that have not yet become thoroughly combined-such is the social condition of Mexico, notwithstanding that four hundred years ago, the Spaniards, although introducing themselves as a new element of complexity, still brought

forth the first organized effort to blend the different peoples into one faith, one rule, one purpose. The blending process is yet unfinished either because human nature opposes such tendencies as are imposed upon it through force or because the conflicting elements are so deeply differentiated that even religion has found the task a hard and lengthy one. Let us now set aside for a moment the racial question in order to consider the nature of the soil. A glance at our physical structure will only add to the puzzle of the Mexican problem. A sort of elongated, immensely vast pyramid, cut at the top end, then sloping toward the two seas. On the top a temperate climate fit for the pine, the wheat, and the corn, and as you go down, all the varieties of plants and of animals, together with the unexplored unlimited wealth of the tropical jungle. All climates and all resources, just as amongst the people you will find all sorts of faces-the white man's face represented by the gallego and the asturiano of modern Spain and by the descendants of the old Castilian and the gay Andalusian—the oldtime gentlemen and landowners who are gradually absorbed in blood and in temperament by the ascending indigenous wave of the mestizo and the Indian. Standards of living also multiply and coexist,

from wealth and refinement to absolute des: titution and want. A country of caste and oppositions of every sort, a country of worry and of wonder. Even in respect to moral temperament our lot varies from the saintly deeds of the missionaries to the wretched cruelties of the conquerors, and in latter days from the sternness and enlightenment of a Juarez or a Madero to the brutality of military chieftains who impose political murder as the rule of government. Such is our Mexico, a country of hope and despair; the rhythm of its very life is the rhythm of contrast. The nation where contrast is the rule instead of the exception—such is, I believe, the main trait of our national being. Perhaps the reason of the social contrast lies in the varied physical, temperamental, and historical factors that intervene in the making of our soul. Progress in other lands seems to be a comparatively easy affair, instead of a permanent rhythm of contradictions; a well-regulated series of efforts; an addition of similar elements in order to constitute progress; a constant flow of cumulations instead of the repeated subtractions in which we lose ourselves. For instance—the original United States, with its level, rich soil, all about the same for cultivating purposes from New England to Georgia and to the Middle West; a land open to the

flow of civilization; the tool fit for one place, being simply moved along in increased rate of production. Compare that with Mexico where the climate and the soil and the kind of the tillage change from north to south, from east to west, and within only a few miles around any given spot. Compare also the homogeneous racial stock at the beginning of this country, the unmixed European of the original Eastern colonies, developing in a virgin land; compare that with the hundred different stocks that inhabit the Mexican territory, and you will then understand why it is that our country has not been able to give a crop —it has not had the time necessary to ripen its fruit. But let us say from the beginning that the case of Mexico is not an isolated fact, a national situation; the case of Mexico is a portion of a larger continental situation. The case of Mexico is exactly the same as the case of Bolivia and Peru, of Chile and Venezuela and Central America. In every one of these nations physical conditions and traditions combine to produce exactly the same results. In order to be more exact in our views it will then be necessary to abandon for a moment the nationalistic pattern, which is of a very superficial mold, in order to study the Latin-American civilization in accordance with such natural subdivisions

as spring to sight as soon as we reflect on the question. Take, for instance, the type of culture that is to be found in Peru, Colombia, or Mexico and compare it with the more simple social manner of Argentina or Uruguay and you will have a clear start in the judgment of our problems. Let us speak, then, of a certain whole composed of the high plateau section that comprehends Mexico, Central America, Colombia, Venezuela, Peru, Ecuador, Bolivia, and Chile. Let us also imagine as one continuous portion all of the lowland occupied by Argentina, Uruguay, and Brazil. The moment we grasp the contrast of these two geographically defined sections of our continent we are in a position to judge from a point of view of reality far more significant than by reference to the political subdivisions. Let us insist upon the outline of these two natural divisions of our America, and let us connect them with a view of the northern section of the New World. We shall have, then, in the west the long highland country extending from New Mexico to Chile; then at both ends of the continent, and more or less in all of its eastern section, notice the expanse of the lowland countries that comprehends the larger part of Canada, the United States in the north, and Argentine, Uruguay, and Brazil in the south.

In order to get a more accurate picture let us imagine a provisional map of the continent: a three-color map corresponding to the threefold topographical sections of our continent, or rather to the three sections made by history out of the two large divisions of lowland and highland, the lowland being inhabited by the Anglo-Saxons in the north and by the Latins in the south. We could give color then to our map by spreading, say for instance, a golden yellow over all the section of the highland, considering its closeness to the sun—a few miles of altitude, of nearness to, or of distance from, the sun meaning so much in the schedules of our planet. After covering up with yellow all this highland section, we could take a green color to indicate the fertile plains of the Amazonas and the Pampas, and then we could put a vivid pink upon the surface of Northeastern America, from the edge of the California-Colorado plateau, way down to Florida and up to Quebec. Before going any farther we shall remark that there is a complete similarity between the green and the pink areas, especially in the northern and southern ends. The Canada-United States northern section has practically the same sort of soil as the Argentine and Southern Brazil territory. Both are lowland countries of temperate climate, level

surface, and unlimited possibilities for cultivation. The natural problems of both countries are practically the same. Take, for instance, the wheat-growing industry; after you have succeeded in applying the motor plow and the chemical fertilizer, the only thing left is to extend your system and multiply it indefinitely from the Kansas plain to the Argentine pampa. In other words, the technique of civilization will not have to change in going through the enormous surface of the lowland continent. Between the northern and the southern sections there is only one factor of difference, a factor large enough though to justify the different shadow of color in our map. As everybody knows it is the Anglo-Saxon race that has created the astounding North American civilization that is changing the axis of history from the Old World to the New. On the other hand, we have in the south a curiously similar sociological situation, developing under identical natural circumstances, but with the Latin instead of the Anglo-Saxon stamina. For it is Euro- , mixture of European stocks, that pean races, a have been building Southern Brazil and the Pampas empire; but they are predominantly Southern Europeans instead of Northern Europeans, and the results thus obtained in the south can very well be compared with those that were

accomplished in a similar period in the north. If you consider, for instance, the rapid development of territories like San Paulo of Brazil, if you study the figures of town and factory increase, you immediately realize that the fabulous rise of the American Middle West is being matched both agriculturally and industrially by the Latin inhabitants of Brazil, who are working under conditions similar in nature to the North American conditions. Only the fact that the Latin spirit predominates in the lowland of the south while the Anglo-Saxon spirit rules the north will justify our provisional three-colored division of the map of our continent. The threefold division is in reality only a provisional one, because we have in the center of the continent, or rather in the center of the lowlands of the continent, a huge area that falls in the realm of what we know as the tropical country-the hot country, practically unconquered yet by man. In fact the distinction is so important that the whole question of civilized life in the tropics should be undertaken as a separate problem. We shall have to point out in our map and consequently we shall have to imagine a fiery color spread over the surface of the whole section composed of the coast of Mexico and all of the Antilles, plus the coast of

Central America, Venezuela, and all of the Amazonas territory. Although we shall not go very deeply into the discussion of the tropical problem, let us say in passing that it is probably the most vital problem for the future of our whole continent-perhaps even the most vital for the future of humanity at large. The mere idea of the possibility of mastering the tropical climate and resources open before our imagination some thing like the eve of a new epoch in human culture. A period is bound to come in which humanity, duly provided with a powerful technique, will undertake the conquest and exploitation of the torrid zone. With a highly developed equipment, man will start in the south a task similar to what was done thousands of years ago when, through the invention of fire and the use of combustion, the wild hunter succeeded in mastering and adapting for civilization the snow-covered plains of the cold and the temperate zones. The complete outline of our map will have to be redrawn; the whole process of history will change on the same day that we shall become capable of handling cold waves and chemical processes, and able to enter into the jungles of Brazil and Colombia and Mexico to impose there the rule of man and the purpose of man. But

it would take us too far away if we stop to consider the possibilities of this sort of task. Let us only mention the fact of the existence of these four natural sections in our continent, insisting a little further upon the problem of the nations located in what we have called the highland as compared with the future of the nations living in the lowlands of the two ends of the New World and which constitute two undisputed successes—the colossal success of the United States and the Canadian Empire and the rapidly increasing success of the Brazil-Argentina Latin civilization. First we shall try to compare the northern type of homogeneous culture with the southern type of homogeneous culture, and after that we will pass judgment on the heterogeneous, composite type of culture represented by the highland and the tropical nations. It is easy to notice from the start, that the differences between Anglo-Saxon North America and Latin South America are only racial, temperamental, spiritual differences. The material problems of both civilizations are very similar if not the same. Both civilizations are governed by the normal law of associated kindred efforts that combine to build a great nation. None of the two lowland territories has suffered from the tragic rhythm of contrast

which we have pointed out as being the rule of the highland type of civilization. This alone explains why the Latin and the Anglo-Saxon, although so different in temperament, have yet succeeded in creating, each one in its own area, that wonder of the New World-the possibility of populations and cities developing overnight. The truth is that there is nothing extraordinary in this sort of achievement. Take any moderately capable branch of the human tamily, give it tertile plains and rivers to carry its boats and its crops and you will be repeating the old-time story of every regular normal civilization. If to these favorable surroundings you add a certain number of good seaports, then sooner or later there will arise one of those outgrowing cultures that have created the fabric of modern life. There has never been any considerable doubt expressed as to the future of Argentina, just as nobody doubted fifty years ago that the Yankees were bound to create a strong modern nation. Where the problem was to enlarge and multiply the prairies of England and the herds of Scotland, all that was required was a sort of cumulative effort, one generation adding naturally to the work of the other generation and everybody contributing to the increase of the unlimited figures of a prosperity that could be calculated beforehand. It is

very easy to collect results from a territory of such a sort. It is very easy to be a prophet where all the elements of a national growth are given as fixed normal elements. The same can be said of temperate Argentina. Humanity has tried once and again, and always with a fair measure of success, all of this cumulative process of civilization where nothing is left to chance or to fate. But the task changes in scope and in nature the moment you leave the trodden road to enter into the trackless unknown of uncontrollable natural elements. It is then, perhaps, not so much a question of race capacities as it is mainly the nature of the territory and the peculiar task of every given period of history that one should have in mind in order to judge fairly on a given situation. To make this point even more clear, allow me to give you an instance taken from the present condition of our own American continent. It very often has been said that the Spanish system of colonization has proved to be a failure because none of the old Spanish-American colonies has been able to compete with the astounding progress of the United States. For some reason or other almost everybody accepts the belief that the Spanish system of colonization and culture cannot compare with its rival, the English system of

colonization in America. But when you start to investigate the reasons of such supposed failure, immediately not one but a hundred facts and circumstances spring up to demonstrate that the Spanish encountered and solved difficulties such as never appeared before the English invader. We shall not undertake to consider this historical question, but judging the problem even by our present standards there is a very significant question that I have once before submitted to a learned audience. The question is the following: Why is it that the English, the Dutch, and the French, three firstclass races, have had such slight success in their sleepy old colonies of the three Guianas? What have these three powerful races done in their South American lot? They have done considerably less than what the Spaniards did in the similar surrounding territories of Venezuela and Yucatan and the coast of Mexico. Why is it then that the three all-gifted nations of Northern Europe have failed in the same territories where Spain was able to achieve a considerable amount of success? Does this instance not show at least that perhaps we have been too quick to underestimate the civilizing effort of the Spaniard in tropical America, instead of realizing that our civilization as a whole is not yet prepared to meet the obstacles of heat and big

rivers and unfavorable elements? And notice further that the Guianas are a virgin country while Mexico and the rest of the highland country is not a virgin territory, not a barren, empty zone, but a land more complicated precisely because it is filled with residues of past civilizations, haunted with phantasms of noble failures that call to our will for a new opportunity of development. Again coming back to the lowland type of civilization represented by the Anglo-Saxon and the Latin nations at opposite ends of the continent, let us say also that, although both have in common the temperate climate and the consequent homogeneous type of civilization, there is still between them a difference in spiritual nature which is bound to give different, though in each case very admirable, results. It is hard to define any social subject with any amount of fairness because every definition implies a more or less arbitrary selection of certain features at the expense and to the exclusion of others. It would take volumes, simply to try to point out what we mean when we speak of the Latin temperament transplanted to America and what we mean by the Anglo-Saxon of the New World. But taking for granted that our statements will have to be incomplete and sometimes overdrawn, we are bound

to repeat that there exists a deep, important difference between the people of Latin America and the people of Anglo-Saxon America. The difference is so much more important because it is a difference of a spiritual sort. Perhaps it lies in the manner of feeling and in the manner of expressing our feelings of life. It is in the type of our higher desires and in the manner we go about our pleasures that we can best be distinguished one from the other. The physiological, the elementary material needs of our nature are practically the same in all the human family; we all need food and shelter, but the moment the practical need is quieted through satisfaction or control, and as soon as we conquer leisure, a series of different longings and desires will arise. What is a pleasure to me, may not be a pleasure to others; and such things as delight a certain kind of people may displease or embarrass another. In the manner of enjoying life-there is where the thinker should search; where the artist should discover those traits that enable him to portray the soul of a nation or a period. And when one speaks of pleasure, one naturally has to take up the literature, the art, the emotion, the soul-lifting expres sions of a country and its epoch. In the manner of enjoying life and in the manner of expressing the

higher purposes of life the Latin and the Anglo-Saxon of America are different, just as the two parental races are different in the old continent. And it is only natural that this should be so, because we are a sort of readaptation of the Mediterranean standards and manners of life while the North Americans are a sort of enlarged Baltic civilization. And the fact that European civilization is a solidly inspired forward movement of humanity, notwithstanding the internal differences of Europe-indeed exactly on account of those internal differences—should teach us in America that it is possible to build a strong powerful civilization of the New World without trying to impose one type of civilization upon the other, without trying even to argue which is the better, whether the Latin or the Anglo-Saxon; for both are useful, and perhaps both are indispensable for the present and the future power and glory of the continent. It is not by suppressing differences that progress opens its way; it is through differences—deeply inspired, sincere differences-that the human soul has made all of its conquests. And the explanation is a very simple one: it is only material differences that create bitterness and rivalry among men. Spiritual differences on the contrary tend to the tightening of human bonds, because we find pleasure in every

difference of the taste; and every peculiarity enriches the wealth of the species. In itself spiritual wealth is such that everybody can enjoy it without using it up, but on the contrary the more you make use of it the richer in value it becomes. The fact that this continent is divided among Anglo-Saxons and Latins should be looked upon then as a blessing; because we all long for a higher, richer spiritual world, and it is only through the work of singularly gifted groups of people that a true all-comprehending type of civilization may come to life. The bigoted patriot who may dream of an all-Yankee America extending its shops from Patagonia to Canada is just as potent a foe to the true ends of mankind as the blind Latin-American chauvinist who may dream of a time of decay in which the Yankee standards of life are to be substituted by the newer southern manners of life. The one comforting fact is that differences of temperament and of soul tend to create sympathy and friendliness rather than opposition and scorn, and this should be borne in mind whenever any conflict of a material character may arise among our nations. The other evident fact is the oneness of the temperamental type of the people living south of the Tropic of Cancer. In the south we are one, morally and racially,

and this unity is not destroyed through our threefold geographic, ethnographic map, just as the Colorado Mountains do not break the Yankee spirit of the northern country. Fortunately some peculiarities and modes of expression of the soul do not follow slavishly the boundaries and varieties of the soil. The highland has its own problems, and the tropic has its own problems; but above this a similar cultural tradition maintains a perfect unity between the people of the Antilles and those of the Mexican Plateau, who constitute an almost identical type with the inhabitants of Argentina, Chile, or Peru. In other words we might again present the problem by saying that the Latin culture is represented in America by the three geographical working zones we have been defining: the peculiar highland, the tropical land, and the southern lowland inhabited by Latins. If we were to draft a soul-map of the continent instead of the working map we have been mentioning, then we should have to use just one color from the Rio Grande to the Tierra del Fuego, including the Antilles, and another color for the United States and Canada; and thus we would have before us the two forms of civilization, the two manners of interpreting life, that we must try to combine in a brotherly manner if our purpose is as it should be, to create in this

hemisphere a new cycle of history-the cycle of liberty, understanding, and love amongst all races and nations. But again, as soon as we start to consider what Latin America really is we fall fatally into the three subdivisions already outlined—subdivisions that very plainly indicate to us the threefold task of our culture. Thus we have, as a map suited to working purposes, the four distinctive zones, the four cultural zones of the New World: (I) the North American, Anglo-Saxon zone of the United States and Canadian lowlands; (2) the highland or Sierra Madre, Andean Plateau of temperate climate and mixed Indian-Spanish populations; (3) the torrid, or tropical, zone consisting of Cuba, Santo Domingo, and Puerto Rico, plus the coast of Mexico and Central America and the hot low countries of Venezuela and Colombia, with the immense unexplored zone of the Amazonas and the Orinoco; (4) and farther south, the Latin lowlands of Argentina and Brazil. I have called this fourfold subdivision a working subdivision, and neither the name nor the classifications are arbitrary; on the contrary they both correspond exactly to living undeniable realities. We all know that the richest, vastest, most promising soil of the New World lies in the Torrid Zone,

a place where nobody has yet been able to live and to prosper. This presents a task that will come into execution in some future time, perhaps close to our day, perhaps still distant; but let us have in mind that the race that shall conquer the tropics will be the master of the future. In regard to Latin-American problems we must consider that one of Latin-America's greatest handicaps has been this inheritance of the tropical zone-an inheritance that may develop tomorrow into untold wonders, but that today stands as a weight on our shoulders and as a barrier to our effort. It is time now to consider the problem of the highland as it appears, for instance, in Mexico. We find that Mexico, as we have already pointed out, is a mixture of climates, of races, and cultures; but still more perplexing it happens that Mexico is the zone where nature has put, one opposing the other, the two most powerful but least controllable elements: the tropical heat and the mountain. From whatever way you approach the problem of civilization in Mexico you will find the strength of these two formidable barriers of human enterprise: excessive heat in certain sections, impassable mountains in other places. We have already stated that the tropical heat may be converted in some near future into an advantage instead of a handicap.

Can we say the same of the mountain? I believe we can; but, of course, not under the present almost elementary condition of human technique. Mexico is one of the most mountainous countries in the world; wherever you go, excepting only the northern end of the plateau, you encounter the sierra; you meet with the mountain in all its grandeur and its charm, with all its majesty and its might. Hard indeed it seems to establish any degree of civilized standards in the midst of a nature that seems adapted for the bird rather than for man. Building roads in such a territory, as well as tunnels, means such a terrific effort that the whole system of man's labor seems checked and postponed the very moment that you meet with the masses of the Cordillera. The best proof that we have not entirely overcome, even with our minds, all of this awe and power of the mountain, can be found in the emotion with which we read today historical accounts of the crossing of the Alps by Hannibal, or the crossing of the Andes by Bolivar's armies. If the occasional feat of transporting through the mountains is still considered an admirable enterprise, imagine what it means to be forced to establish a regular road-system through the ravine and the summit. Imagine what it means to be #25]

forced to plant and cultivate grain on the slope of the hills, under the menace of ravaging storms. If we consider then that Mexico, like Peru and Bolivia and Colombia, is a sort of meeting place of all of the most powerful and yet uncontrolled elements of nature the sierra and the heat, the flood and the earthquake-and if we add to these natural handicaps to the ways of man the other conflicting factors of race and history, we shall readily understand the reason for the continued and colossal failures of civilized effort in our country. And after reflecting upon these circumstances, will there be anybody bold enough to condemn a race or a series of races that have been struggling under such exceptionally difficult conditions? Are we not, on the other hand, authorized to state that we are working under the pressure of a series of obstacles and hardships such as no other people have ever encountered? At least we must seek in the existence of all of these handicaps the reason for many of our national traits, both the bad and the good traits. Take, for instance, our individual, our national psychology. We have been raised in the mountains; we have been living out of the mountains—that is to say, we have been depending on mining for our living and our prosperity. From Potosí to Zacatecas and

Guanajuato the highland of America, together with the northern end of California, has been supplying the world with silver and gold. Our forefathers, after completing the conquest, devoted themselves to the extraction of the ore from the vein. They did this under the same risky, bold circumstances with which they had carried on the conquest of the land. Mining at that time was an adventure as doubtful as the expeditions and combats for the discovery of the Eldorados. Conquerors, discoverers, explorers of the unknown surfaces of the continent, and later miners who explored the unknown underground in search of Aladdin's wealth-all of them were adventurous heroes with' uncertain tasks to fulfil. It is only natural that such ways of living should have affected the feeling of the race toward life. People that get into the habit of adventure necessarily develop traits of imagination and occasional daring followed by long periods of relaxation—traits such as are necessary for their particular form of living. In some respects the national character becomes spoiled; we become accustomed to await everything ; from the unexpected. Our psychology as a rule is the psychology of the gambler; we gamble with our wealth and with our chances in life; in fact, we even gamble with our lives. A popular saying is often applied

whenever we hesitate before unknown, possibly unexpected, developments: A ver que sale, "Let us see what comes out of it." By it we mean not fatalism but a sort of a lottery sentiment, a decision to try fate and to force it to give out its secret and its treasure. The A ver que sale really means: "Let us put faith in the outcome; after we have done our best let the uncontrollable do its caprice." Such is our normal attitude toward life; such was the attitude of the explorer of the wilderness and the attitude of the miner of the latter day. Such is the attitude imposed on man by the mountain and by all uncontrolled forces of nature. A similar psychology might be traced perhaps even in the Yankee miner of the first epoch because nature imposed its influence upon man in this wild mysterious highland of the New World. There is a sort of sentiment which one might call the bonanza sentiment, which pervades our soul with all the strength of enthusiasm but also with the deteriorating effect of dismay of the present and doubt about the future. All the effects of the mountain upon man are far-reaching. The civilizations of the plains go along increasing through centuries in an added enjoyment of wealth that is only interrupted by war and jealousy of less fortunate neighbors. But a 11281

civilization like the civilization of our highland which has been dependent on the mining industry cannot be permanent, cannot be more permanent than the industry to which it owes its breath. Even the city that the miner builds is a temporary city. Placed as a rule on the slopes of the hills that surround the mining camp, the city has to bring from afar and has to pay dearly for its food and its water. It does not matter when the times are prosperous, but a collapse becomes inevitable the very moment the vein is exhausted. And after the vein is exhausted no attachment can be maintained with the soil, the mining area as a rule being unfit for cultivation. There is then nothing left to do but to emigrate, or at least to come down to the more hospitable valley, there to start anew, undergoing poverty after the days of lavish expenditure and splendor. Even the only remaining testimony of good times is condemned to become a ruin. I refer to the gorgeous churches, to the handsome palaces that fill such old towns as Guanajuato of Mexico and Quito of Ecuador, so many marks of the height of the bonanza wave. The overflow of gold, after spreading all over the world, finds its level in the safes of the calculating lowland agricultural and industrial people, who had the patience necessary to create savings and to organize banks. Only in

architecture, the most noble of arts, has the miner been able to leave the permanent trace of his wandering but princely masterful soul. If, for instance, California was saved the fate of Guanajuato or Potosí, it is only due to the fact that California instead of being surrounded by unsolved riddles of the tropic found itself inside the permanent civilization of the Middle West; its present agricultural wealth being only an extension of the neighboring highly developed lowland standard of work. Left alone it would have probably fallen into the curse of the highland, into the irregular, perplexing rhythm of the brightness and shadow of ardent hopes and painful despair-the law of contrasts that constitutes the rule of life in the plateau. What is, then, the conclusion that we should draw from such circumstances? Should we state that the soil of Mexico and the soil of the highland are unfit for a true civilization, for a powerful civilization, and are consequently bound to the tragedy of flashing prospects and then irrevocable decay? How could we account then for the fact that Mexico and Peru, during the seventeenth and the early eighteenth centuries, were the centers of the only civilization then existing on the continent - a civilization that created an architectural

style like the Mexican churriguera that today is giving inspiration to the most important development of the present-day North American architecture; a civilization that printed the first books and issued the first newspapers of the continent; that built roads through the desert extending from the Mexican Plateau to the wild immense plains of Arizona and New Mexico; a civilization and a national wealth that had the power to overflow its territory in order to contribute to the building of forts and palaces in such distant places as the island of Puerto Rico and the missions of California? How could such an effort come to naught by break and fall? And, first of all, how did it happen to achieve what it did achieve? All of these perplexing questions are easily understood by those who have been in Mexico, by those who have felt the fascination of the highland power. The explanation lies in that same law of contrast and irregularity, in that rhythm of the unexpected possibilities and calamities-the law to which I have been referring as peculiar to the civilization of the highland. It is not only the bonanza that intervenes to create among us periods of renascence and forescence and periods of decay; it is all of the factors of nature combined, that lead in Mexico to this constant

uncertainty and to the corresponding periodical offspring of the higher capacities of life. The mountain and the climate constitute a handicap to steady, regulated progress, but the mountain and the climate also constitute a treasure. The highland succeeded when it devoted itself to its proper task, the task of mining; but when it was found necessary through the exhaustion of the mine or through changed conditions in the world-market to change from the mine industry to the agricultural or the manufacturing industry, it was found that we lacked in the highland most of the essential equipment. We had no irrigation works to protect our planted fields from the irregularities or the scarcity of rainfall; we had no combustible, no coal, to generate the steam that moved factories. For the moment-and in the life of nations centuries are like mere moments-for a moment we found ourselves in the midst of a world that had changed its tools without giving us notice. Absorbed as we were, and even infatuated with our wealth in silver and gold, we did not realize that an era was developing in which coal and steel would become more valuable than gold and would succeed in putting to its service all the gold of our mines and of the world's mines. And perhaps the main reason for the evident decay we have shown in this last century

comes from the fact that we did not have at hand the gold of our times-steel and steam working together for the new period of worldculture. Our mining industry in such a situation became nothing but a luxury; and it is always the powerful, the vitally powerful, that makes the terms for the value of any luxury, Since then we have not found our way economically. It takes time and it takes suffering to change the mode of living of any people, and it is always harder to imitate than to invent. Even the ability for inventing goes along with economic demand and success. At the time of the supreme importance of the precious-metal industry, we had in Mexico the most advanced technical methods of the time. The best methods for assaying and smelting ores were local Mexican inventions. In later days how could we be expected to invent in mechanics, if we hardly knew the modern machines except through pictures in books and magazines? It is not then so much a question of race ability as a ques tion of the world-importance of the task that every nation is undertaking in a certain given time. In the period of the adaptation of motor power to human industry we have had to be spectators. But the question now is: What is this new tool in the hands of man going to mean for us? May it not

possibly happen that such tools, though not originated in our territory, are still apt to render a large profit in our lands, larger even than in the place of their origin? It is true that our case might have appeared to be hopeless when machinery was moved only by steam power. We had neither the stuff out of which a mechanical civilization is made nor the necessary useful combustible. But the very instant that modern industry began to utilize electrical power instead of steam power, the whole aspect of the future changed to our benefit. Because what other country in the world can rival Mexico in the lavish, immeasurable amounts of utilizable energy that today goes to waste in the annual, natural rhythm of the fogs that rise from the sea in order to make the clouds, and the wind that takes the clouds over the mountain tops in order to cover the plateau with a rainfall that comes rushing down, every season, through the narrow passes of the ravines and through the saltos of the thousand grades of levels? And every one of these changes in level is like an inexhaustible coal mine— a perpetual source of energy, that will allow us to build, some day, one of the most potent manufacturing centers of history. So in this way, in our land of mystery and contrast, the mountain that has been a handicap is apt to become, tomorrow,

just the treasure that is needed to give comfort and power to a great wonderful epoch. Plans for the industrial electrification of countries are now discussed everywhere, but there is probably no other section of the world that is more fit for this sort of advancement than Mexico; and notice, if you will, that this advantage comes to us precisely in the combinations of the two disadvantages that appeared to be fatal-the heat and the mountain. For if it were not for the heat, the clouds could not carry mountains of water to be dropped over the mountain of rock, producing thus the electrical current that is there waiting for the mastery of man. It is enough to consider the unlimited possibilities of a development of the sort just outlined in order to understand that Mexico is not a hopeless backward country, but a wonderful promise—more than that, a certainty that can not be delayed very much longer. The hour of Mexico has not yet sounded, but it is there already marked in the clock of progress. The hour of the whole of the highland will be a wonderful hour. So long as electricity remains the governing power of human industry, the highland will be able to retain the leadership among nations. It would take endless space and thought to follow

all the different factors that contribute to the distinction of the highland and the lowland, to describe what civilization means in a country like Mexico and what it means in a flat country like Argentina or Western United States; all that we can do, for the present, is to bring the main characteristics to the attention of the hearer. There are many other elements that contribute to mark the differences between the highland and the lowland, between Mexico and, for instance, Argentina and Eastern United States. The most important of these elements after the physical characteristics already discussed is the racial element. The racial element of the highland is different from the racial element of the lowland. We have already referred to the fact that the United States is racially a mixture of Northern European bloods while Argentina and Southern Brazil are composed of Southern European stock. The highland is more complex on account of the Indians, or rather on account of the different races of Indians that inhabit it; and also on account of the mestizo, who as everybody knows came into existence through the mixture of the Spanish and the Indian bloods. It has often been repeated that the reason for the slow progress of Bolivia and of Mexico, for instance, is due to the large Indian population of

both of these highland countries. Such a statement involves never ending questions of race-aptitude and biological, anthropological theories. One cannot deny the fact that the Indian lives in a backward condition from the economical point of view. But whenever one compares sincerely the mental aptitude or the moral qualities of the Indian with the other races of the world one is convinced that the Indian is the possessor of as many good qualities as any other living race. You will easily realize that, if you apply truly superior standards of judgment. I know the extent of race prejudice, but is it not the duty of the mind to study dispassionately and draw its conclusions in accordance with a sense of the higher meaning of life? And is not the race question, however you approach it, one in which almost any statement receives credence? A thing that happens only because we know little about it! Observe, though, the handicraft of the Indian; observe it in the architecture of the prehistoric times; and watch it at work in the present-day small industry of the mountain-section villages. A nation that is capable of exercising such complicated and artistic workmanship is also capable of producing any sort of mechanical, industrial manufacture. And when such a race will get the machinery

necessary for large-scale production, we may be sure that the native instinct for refinement and beauty will leave its imprint even in the rude results of the steel production, in the same manner that today it takes a refined worker, an artist, to complete and polish the pieces of the most powerful delicate air-motor. There is not one side of the question in which different views cannot be advanced. Take, for instance, a question apparently trivial—the question of good looks. The main reason why most people retain their race prejudices is because a certain aesthetical instinct leads us to search for beauty in our fellow-beings. The white race, the predominant race of today, often finds that the other racial types are ugly. The other racial types may not always find that the white man is a sort of god descended from the sun; but still, as a rule, they allow themselves to be fascinated by the white man's standards of beauty. You find almost in every one of our Indian or mestizo poets, dark of skin themselves, the ardent eulogy of the white hands and the pale cheeks of the amada. This aspiration toward the white standard of beauty may be only one of the consequences of the fact that the white race is predominant in the present era of history. To be sure the blond-pink type of beauty, popular

today, was not known nor hardly admired by the pale Egyptian, whose skin, stained by the sun, had in its shade something of the shimmer of alabaster before a light. The standards of beauty change with the times and the people; but there is one thing probably certain and it is that physical beauty is closely related to comfort and peace of mind. In other words, a race of slaves cannot be beautiful because hard work and misery tend to leave their imprint on the body. There is not in all Europe a prettier stock than that Celtic Portuguese race that produces some of the best flavored wines of the world. And yet I have seen thousands of really ugly peasant women, whose faces, although enlightened with the Minervan green eyes of the most aristocratic of races, have fallen in true degradation through hard constant toil in the open field. It is no wonder, then, that a large proportion of the Indian population is decidedly plain looking. Where there is no comfort at all, the human body turns back to the beasts. Leisure and wealth develop beauty in any racial stock. Among the Indian races one often finds, under the common trait of a more or less dark brown skin, all the varieties of expression from the oddest and ugliest to most perfect Caucasian lines. Many a voyager knows the fascination of the Tehuana Indian,

whose charm resembles the effect of a heavy odorous wine. The racial problems we are mentioning in a passing way are accentuated in the highland but are not entirely peculiar to the highland. Argentina and Brazil reach and take into their bosom extensive provinces like Tucuman and El Chaco or Parana and Misiones in which racial conditions are very similar to the Mexican or the Bolivian conditions. It would then be absurd to think that the purely Latin European people of the Argentine coast were going to constitute a caste apart from the mestizo and the Indian of the interior. Such a thing would be as ignoble as to become Argentinian in order to persist as a porteño—a citizen of Buenos Aires. The process there, just as in the rest of Latin America, is of amalgamation with the native stock. The descendants of the Italian and the Pole in one or two generations become criollos, and thus fall into the common type of the continental Latin-American civilization. In this way, gradually, and notwithstanding nature's differences in soil and climate, we are becoming more and more identical. We are bound together by a common past, a common tongue, a common culture, and even our institutions and our problems are the same from the moral and spiritual point of view.

With the obstacles of nature we have always counted, but at the same time the very principle of our faith was defined when Bolivar, referring to the Latin American union stated: If nature opposes we shall conquer nature. The time is nearing when the tropic will be mastered and when the intricacies of the highland will be converted into usefulness. We have a world-mission to fulfil. The task involves such a tremendous effort that we do not pretend that we are going to develop, alone, all this new era of history. We know that today more than ever the work of civilization requires the concerted effort, the collaboration of every human being no matter from whence he comes. Our standard then should be a free open standard-free not only from the point of view of public rights but also free from prejudice, free through its wide power of brotherly emotion—a free heart, strong, and always ready for all sorts of love. In order to sum up the nature of our progress as compared with that of the United States let us state that North America has developed in accordance with a law of similarity of races and efforts and conditions while Latin America is struggling along according to a sort of varying rhythm of ⟦6⟧ radical changes and contrasts. The law of similarity and the law of contrast—which one is more rich in truly lofty human achievement is a question that only the future, only a comparatively remote future, can tell.

A vital question in Latin America, and one that is often debated is this: Should all the Latin-American states remain loyal to their written constitutions dating from the beginnings of the nineteenth century that establish the sovereignty of the people expressed by the vote, or is it better to look for more native standards such as military dictatorships in the name of the republic or in the name of socialism? Let us say from the start that the question is only debated in such places as have to suffer from the military dictators and from those people that wish to please the military dictators. It would not be fair to state that Argentina or Brazil have any sort of sympathy for military rule; both of them are too civilized to compare even in theory the imperfect rule of democracy—imperfect though as it is——with the troglodite methods of our military dictators. But if Argentina and Brazil and Colombia and Cuba and Costa Rica succeeded in getting rid, fifty years ago, of personal leadership and dictatorship of the type we call "caudillism" — the rule of the military—there is another large group of nations

where local petty caesarism is constantly reasserting itself and maintaining hold, through ignorance, through cowardice, through lies, and through murder and theft. And as the question of passing judgment on such methods of government, when applied to our lands, is not only discussed by local talent but also very often advocated by enlightened foreigners, I wish to take advantage of the hospitality of this University of Chicago—a hospitality generously granted to truth and the good cause of human understanding—in order to present a few suggestions to contradict the opinion of those that are constantly talking of the iron hand and the strong oneman rule that is supposed to achieve success in our more backward Latin-American countries. The struggle between democratic methods and dictatorial methods of government is not a new one in our continent. The Indians of pre-Cortesian times were slaves to god-like dictators, that governed the state in a manner, very similar to the manner of modern military caudillos. The monarch of old represented the state; the caudillo of the times of Santa Anna represented liberalism or centralism; and the caudillo and dictator of today represents order, for instance, in Venezuela, or radicalism in Mexico. At bottom they all represent the

one-man savage rule of the Oriental type of despotisms of yesterday and of today. In fact, there is very little difference between a Sikh pascha of Asia and a soldier-president of Latin-American history -the difference consisting in that the people of Latin America have never tolerated a long dictatorship and have always succeeded in punishing the dictator, through liberating triumphant revolutions. But revolution again brings into power the victorious revolutionist chieftain, and again we fall into the old ways and the same abuses; and so democracy, that in many cases has not even been tried, is scolded and ridiculed, only to serve better the shameful interests of one-man rule. Such has been the development of events, but the one thing we should try to rescue from all this tragedy is the validity and the usefulness of a certain number of principles without which no nation can survive; and among these principles the democratic form of government is one of the most essential. One of the puzzles of old Mexican history and of old Peruvian history is the facility with which a small group of adventurers succeeded in overturning and subduing the all-powerful empires of the Aztecs and the Incas. And yet if we give the matter a moment's attention we shall find the simple lesson

that history once and again repeats for us in its pages—the lesson which says that a despotism can never survive in a clash with a democracy. All of you remember the classical story of Sparta and Athens defeating the huge armies of despotism under Darius, the incarnate state and God of the Persians. A free parliament appointing generals that commanded free men; citizens of small republics, but subject to no man-these were enough to destroy the most powerful empire of the time. The Spaniards that came to conquer America were a wonderful sort of men, brigands if you like, but free brigands, independent and haughty in their own land. So when they arrived in Mexico and observed the poor Indian, trembling before the mere name of his emperor, the all-powerful Monteexperienced a gay temptazuma, they must have tion to show the poor Indian what the god-like Montezuma was really worth. And they did so, and as soon as Montezuma was captured, the whole empire crumbled, because one-man countries and one-man situations follow the fate of the idol and pay for the sin of man-worship. The Spanish conquerors were the remnants of the army that fought the Arabs under Isabella, and Isabella was the chief of a group of more or less independent kingdoms and towns that had their own fuero, their own municipal

liberties. At the time of Isabella it was yet true that every Spaniard felt he was as good as the king, and any two of them, better than the king, just as the famous saying puts it. So it is evident that the clash between the Indian and the Spaniard in the days of Cortes and Pizarro was a clash between the democracy of the time-one of the most genuine democracies of Europeand despotism— one of the crudest despotisms of history, the despotism of Montezuma and the Inca. I doubt very much that the Spaniards of the time of Philip II would have been able to repeat the enterprise of conquering a world. When a nation is afraid of its own government, very little can be done against a foreign enemy or in a foreign enterprise. And if the feat of these bands of freemen conquering kingdoms of enslaved people is amazing, the way they organized things after the conquest is not less admirable. Every new settlement and every old town was always organized, not in accordance with the indigenous habit of dependence to a certain chief, but in the good Spanish way of organizing a city council. The free and ardent proselytism of the missionary was another civilizing and democratic influence. The religious theory of the Christian, in making us all brothers in God, is the most powerful ratification of democratic doctrines.

And it was only in the later days, in the days of decay, in the days of emperors that had made no conquests, emperors by chance like Charles V and monsters like Philip I, it was only then that the king's envoy, and the judge of the inquisition, began to degrade and corrupt the wonderful original organization. Still, the undoubted fruition of Spanish culture in the America of the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries was due to the comparatively democratic methods of government and to the fair-minded and liberal policies of such viceroys as Hurtado de Mendoza and the Revillagigedos, who were men with the modern concept and vision of government, according to whom government is a service and a duty toward the community and not a privilege and a joy of the despot. But with Spanish decay and with Spanish despotism at home, the colonies gradually came down to the same low political standard: The King and the Church-the King represented by the soldier, and the Church represented by the Inquisition. Both, closely allied, became supreme and governed unopposed to the misfortune of the people. And when the War of Independence broke out, it was the spirit of the old Spanish fuero that revived in the race; we wanted to be free as our fore- 11481

fathers had been free in the old communes of Castilla and Zaragoza; communes where even the rule of the Roman emperor had been very careful not to offend the sentiments of citizenship. Many of our liberators were men of purely Spanish blood, liberty-loving souls, with the old Spanish haughtiness. Many others of our liberators were mestizos who had in their souls the love of a past that was, at least in part, their own inheritance. And the pure Indians that fought our War of Independence were also men that had adapted and adopted the European standard of social life-the Christian standard of social arrangement, according to which one man is, or can be, just as worthy as the other and is entitled not only to the same rights but even to a certain amount of protection if he happens to be weak or destitute. Our War of Independence from Spain was then. a huge democratic upheaval of the mestizo and the Indian race of America. And it shows that the Spanish civilizer had succeeded in changing the social feelings of the native. When the situation in Spain became such that people had to choose between the degenerate Fernando and Cortes de Cadiz, a Congress of Patriots, all of Spanish America, aligned itself with the men of Cadiz that wanted to re-establish the democratic traditions in Spain.

When these patriots were defeated in Spain, the colonies of America decided to go on with the struggle for themselves; and many of the patriots of Cadiz, Spanish though they were, truly patriotic Spanish, came over to New Spain and to Argentina to create liberated new countries, democratic countries. And our forefathers succeeded in liberating Spanish America from the rule of the Hapsburg-Bourbon degenerate caste —but they did not succeed in establishing working democracies in our nations. The liberators did their task on the battlefield and accomplished their duty through the promulgation of constitutions copied more or less from the democratic standard of the North American Constitution. But revolutions contain in their own dynamics a sort of fatal element of decay and reaction. Very seldom do the men that think and organize and fight for a revolution actually come into power. The struggle eats up the life, or at least the energies, of the initiator and the true revolutionist; and at the end, in the hour of victory, it is the man with • greater shrewdness, the one that took less chances, the one that took best care of himself, that usually is found in the possession of the larger armed group; and then, it is he, the unknown of the struggling period, perhaps the enemy of the original revolutionists,

who comes into power and naturally turns all the reforming spirit of the revolution back again into reaction and pre-war oppression. The instance of Iturbide becoming the head of the Mexican government at the triumph of our War of Independence, after, and notwithstanding, that Iturbide had fought the rebels during ten years and only turned to the rebel banner when the case of Spain was lost, simply demonstrates this rhythm of revolutions in our territory. The present-day Revolution is no exception, as the situation in Mexico to a large extent remains in the hands of people who in many cases antagonized Madero, or at least did not take any part in Madero's uprising. Many of them came into the Revolution, only after Madero had demonstrated that it was a comparatively easy job to overthrow despots; and it is only natural that such people who came to the Revolution, only after it was proved that revolutions were good business, should be trying to imitate Porfirio Diaz's methods of one-man rule rather than Madero's democratic doctrines. But the irrepressible self-asserting revolutionary spirit of the Latin-American nations is enough to show that we shall have no enduring peace on this continent so long as there are one-man governments and dictatorships in our nations. The struggle

of the Latin-American revolutionist is the struggle of democratic European ideas to impose themselves upon the Oriental indigenous type of despotism and upon the decayed soldier-rule of the days of Ferdinand the Coward. All the petty Napoleons of our history, all the Caesars that "have never known defeat," are nothing but incubators of revolutions; and so long as they exist peace cannot exist, because the Latin-American nations are pledged in soul to the democratic ideal of liberty and equality, which is the only basis of any truly civilized form of social arrangement. The first man who really understood the problem of our social development was the Argentine statesman and writer Sarmiento. His views were very clearly and dramatically exposed in a book that should be read carefully by any person who wishes to understand the Latin-American sociology. The book is a novel called Facundo; the hero of the novel, Facundo, is the embodiment of that type of leader that comes when the revolution is over, claiming to be the revolution but only putting in practice, for his own benefit, the same abusive methods of the past. Facundo is the military chieftain who imposes his will through terrorism and does away with the law and with the sense of human sympathy. The only policy of Facundo is the

blood-stained policy of the firing squad: whoever is not with him is against him, and whoever is against him should be shot as enemy of the country or as an enemy of the revolution. With the times, the name of the program changes; but the method does not change. In the time of Facundo the enemies of Facundo were classed as federalistas—defenders of the Argentine federation, and thus were shot. In latter days the enemies of a despot are called enemies of public order and shot, such was the case of the Diaz régimes; in later days the enemies of the military dictator are classified as "reactionaries" and are poisoned or shot; but the system is the same —the system is despotism in one of its more brutal and degraded forms. Sarmiento devoted all his life to eradicate this militarism, this caudillism, from the Argentine soil. And after a long, noble struggle Sarmiento succeeded in gaining control, first, of the educational movement of his country, later, of full power by becoming the president of Argentina. Then Sarmiento, as president, managed to carry along the policy outlined in his novel years before: the policy of Europeanization of Latin America; the policy of democratization of Latin America, as against the policy of the caudillos that are constantly struggling for personal rule. In the ancestral struggle

between democracy and dictatorship, the government of Sarmiento is the first notable success of our continent, and from the success of Sarmiento is derived the present prosperity and greatness of the greatest of the Spanish-American nations, our sister-republic of Argentina. Had the caudillos won, over the intellectual Sarmiento, the situation of Argentina would not be today any better than that of Bolivia; but after the enlightened rule of Sarmiento, the reappearance of the ignorant caudillo was made impossible. The unquestionable success of Argentina has very often been attributed to its temperate climate, to European immigration, to the scarcity of Indian population, etc.; but I believe that the main factor of Argentine's progress is to be found in the victory that Argentina was able to win over the military chieftain, over the caudillo that has ravaged the rest of Spanish America. And my reasons for supporting this opinion are as follows: Argentina herself was unable to take advantage of its temperate climate, wealth, etc., during the long sterile years of the Rosas dictatorship. And it was only when the democratic revolution overthrew the dictatorship that Argentina started to become a nation. Then, if we take in another section of the continent another case of success, perhaps the only case of

permanent success this side of the equator, we find that Costa Rica never has had this type of murderous caudillo that has dishonored the history of other countries. You do not find generals in the annals of Costa Rican history, but since the early. times you find, over there, fairly good schools and a general desire for progress and for civilized human manners of living. Jumping again to the south we find that Chile, a nation that has had no caudillos, no military chieftains in power, has at the same time maintained a very fair standard of progress and a fairly civilized system of government, although in recent years the weight of the reigning oligarchy upon the working classes has become pitifully dangerous. And of course with oppression and backwardness military dictatorship is there, at present, a latent when not an actual calamity. The origin of Chile's greatness lies in the statesmanship of men of the type of Bello, an educator, a grammarian, a man of letters, in power. In Mexico we have always had a fine type of man: the learned man fully prepared with all the advantages of a college career and all the insight of patriotism and even of genius. We had, in the first years of our independent life, a wandering genius Servando de Mier; but the glorious military

caudillos of the time, true ancestors to the present glorious generals of today, kept him out of Mexico off and on for thirty years and succeeded in keeping him away from power. He was undoubtedly unfit to subscribe to the policies of the firing squad and to grab all such property as belongs to the enemies of the "cause," which means the personal enemies of the caudillo of the hour. The only case in which an intellectual group actually came into power in Mexico, in all the history of Mexico, is, at the same time, the only decent period of the history of Mexico and the only progressive period. In fact, it was the time when Mexico was able to write pages into the history of the world; the drama of old-time autocracy and militarism represented by Maximilian, struggling against democracy and right represented by Juarez, has become one of the subjects of the world's literature. The only real progress ever made in Mexico comes also from the time of democracy initiated by Juarez and continued by Lerdo. It was then (remember, this was in the sixties) that the first and the best railroad of the country was built, the first railroads, the first public schools; and, together with material advantages, a complete reform of the social order—a democratic, liberal reform—the organization of public life outside the bonds of the

church; the drafting of educational plans; the establishment of compulsory primary teaching; the moralization of the personnel, and the methods of handling public funds. It has always been noted that the generation of politicians and statesmen that accompanied Juarez in his task after years of public services did not accumulate wealth and never produced the type of the revolutionist hacendado and financier. They did produce splendid financiers like Dublan and Matias Romero, men who reorganized the fiscal systems of the country and brought money into the national treasury after covering all public needs; but they never produced any financier such as military governments develop —the financier who dismisses clerks because he cannot pay the government services and closes schools because it is necessary to economize, but who himself is able to emerge from the absolute destitution of his prepolitical obscurity to the position of millionaire and nouveau riche of an impoverished nation. Most people believe, particularly outside of Mexico, that the most progressive period of our history was due to the iron rule of Porfirio Diaz. I do not deny some of the strong qualities of Porfirio Diaz, particularly after one observes his imitators succeeding by copying all of his vices and none

of his virtues. The main virtue of Porfirio Diaz was personal honesty and decency regarding money affairs; he never used his political power for accumulating wealth; in fact he was a poor man all his life, and only in the later years, during the decay of his rule, did he become wealthy through the presents of subject politicians. But he would not have been able to retain power for such a length of time if he had suffered from that base passion and greed of his later disciples. Admitting then that Porfirio Diaz was probably the best possible type of a despot, yet we shall have to condemn him and his system the moment we stop to think that any despotism of a personal character is limited to the period of life of the despot. And the despot leaving no political inheritors— such as only monarchs can leave —is always unable to take care of the future. So I feel entitled to say to all those defenders of the iron rule, to all the believers in personal rule and caudillism: If you do not want to see another cycle of revolution and chaos, such as the one we are now passing through in Mexico, do not lend any assistance to the personal aggrandizement of any Porfirio Diaz whether spurious or authentic, because every Porfirio Diaz is bound to bring behind him a new era of hate and destruction and chaos.

It is only through democracy that all of our problems will be solved; no other system of government has proved successful anywhere else. The fact that so many of the Latin nations are falling today into the hands of dictators constitutes only a sad sign of decay. Fortunately, we can still turn for comfort toward the most advanced of the Latin nations, to nations like France and Argentina and Brazil. May their example help us and may it be sufficient to restore the confidence of those who believe that we are capable of rising to the standards of free government. One of the most dangerous factors that we have to deal with is the hypocrisy with which we make use of certain names. I prefer the frank dictator who defies public opinion to hypocritical leaders who claim to have respect for certain principles but who go along exercising power from a hiding place and through the hand of some ally or accomplice. The case is beginning to be so frequent in our America, that it is necessary that we should define what is to be understood by democratic government and what is meant by autocratic, militaristic, dictatorial government. The answer is very easy in the case of most of our dictatorships. Our dictatorships distinguish themselves from other countries' dictatorships by I59J

their hypocritical character. Almost all of our dictatorships disguise themselves under the mask of republicanism or under the mask of social reform and radicalism. But the one unequivocal test to differentiate the dictator from the democratic ruler is found in what we call the exercise of facultades extraordinarias "extraordinary powers." The exercise of facultades extraordinarias is equivalent to the decreeing of court-marshall proceedings throughout the nation, and, more than that, because the extraordinary powers in the field of war and human life are always extended to the use of extraordinary powers in finance, which means that any tax can be levied, any confiscation can be made, through the order of the president-dictator alone. It is of no account then that the constitution may guarantee property and life. The constitutional rights are suspended, in order to save public order sometimes, in order to save the revolution on other occasions, in reality only in order to save the personal rule of the despot. Based on this constitutional suspension and on these extraordinary powers in war and finance, citizens are dragged out from their homes by order of a president, to be sent into exile or to face the firing squad. Political parties are dissolved through imprisonment and murder. The press is silenced, the bigger newspapers

go on publishing stories about happenings in Japan and Roumania, but are very careful not to touch on the events of the hour. And then as the crowning victory of the military régime, one day the papers announce that all the properties of the enemies are confiscated in order to pay for the expense of putting down the rebellion or the expense of the prosecution. This last expense is never very considerable as the firing squad is under a regular salary and subject to permanent appointment, as part of an army that is the basis of the caudillo conception of the state. Treaties, international treaties, are concerted with the foreign powers, in which the despot makes exception to the same principles he is supposed to be defending, provided these treaties are accompanied by a wave of persecution of the political enemies that have sought refuge in the foreign land. Large fortunes can be made by the caudillo and his friends through the facultades extraordinarias. How? I shall give you an instance: The facultades extraordinarias in hacienda in finance means that the government can change the tariff from one day to another according to "public needs." With the tariff at his command, on twenty-four hours notice the caudillo becomes a business man. And take for

instance grain, one of those products that are sold at large in the foreign market, in the United States market: when the time of the crop comes, the caudillo decrees a high defensive tariff, a large tax on exportation, "in order to protect the local needs" he will always be careful to state. Naturally the prices of the foodstuff are considerably lowered. It is, then, that the caudillo through some representative, or personally, goes around to the dismayed producers; offers them a little more than the ruinous market price; poses as a protector of their interests; and, as soon as he has got hold of all of the crop, communicates with the finance department. One day, all of a sudden, the public and the producers learn that the tax on exportation of the cereal has been eliminated, in order to protect prices that had become too low, and for the good of the local producer and the public good, as the corresponding decree will always be careful to say. Such things occur repeatedly in the caudillos countries, and they explain by themselves the causes of this fall of production that always accompanies the military rule. It also explains the rapid increase of wealth of the caudillo clan. Men, who in private life had not been able to exceed the level of a second-rate salaried clerk, men who had arrived at the forties without showing any special business

ability suddenly develop what to uninformed observers is a sort of unexpected genius, making millions out of poverty, out of the impoverishment of the producing class. But, of course, there being no free press, public opinion being entirely scared by the regular, pitiless, man-target services of the firing squad, there is nothing left but the abject admiration of a subdued population, hungry and enslaved. Every once in a while, there is in any caudillo country a talk of revolution. As a rule, such talk is very useful to the governing group because it gives it an excuse for a sort of razzia on the enemies' lives and properties. A general confiscation is decreed of the properties of the enemies of public order. Even the savings of widows have in many instances been taken over. The natural consequence of such a system is that nobody cares to invest in the country; even bank deposits flock to foreign safes, going to the United States or to Canada for protection. Take for instance the land question.
