impulses and, guided by education, were transformed almost miraculously from a medieval country into a modern and important nation. Advanced pedagogical methods bore rapid and happy fruit among the Japanese because there was homogeneity, solidarity, and convergent aspirations throughout the national social strata. The new education was unanimously comprehended and embraced as the wedge that would lift the country into its proper place in the world. But the outlook for modern education among the Indo-Hispanic peoples is entirely different. Here are groups heterogenous socially, racially, culturally, and linguistically, with pronounced lack of economic equilibrium. Ethnologically, there are the Indian, the half-breed, and the white—all more or less distinct and separate from each other, and also different in history and tradition. Socially, the Latin-American republics are made up of elements ranging from the most primitive to the ultra-modern; culturally, one finds many different stages of civilization. The principal cities are distinctly modern in their institutions; but outside of them live tribes so little advanced that they make use of practically no pottery or dress, and their ideas have felt the effect of little or no civilizing influence. The same great difference exists linguistically, for besides

the two divisions of Spanish and native, the native division is subdivided into hundreds of languages and dialects. These discrepancies are paralleled economically. Tens of millions of men exist on miserable wages that vary from ten to fifty cents gold, while their millionaire countrymen live princely and useless lives abroad. To further complicate the situation, the governments of these Latin-American countries have nearly always been unstable, for the government, democratic in name only, has had to adapt itself successively and without distinction to the idiosyncracies and the manifestations of the widely varied social groups of the country. One group, exclusive of the rest, triumphed and dominated inevitably, until protest grew strong enough to instal some other power, and so on interminably. Now what educational program could be expected to yield effective results in countries of the typically heterogenous structure here described? For a long time the only program followed at all, and still observed, though of course erroneously, has been that of selecting and applying methods which have proved successful elsewhere—in foreign countries utterly different, and above all far more advanced, as nations. Under this system, those small groups which, due to cultural antecedents—

racial or psychic characteristics-bore some relationship to the foreigners whose methods were adopted, were partly benefited by the exotic transplantation. But the great Indian and half-breed majority gave no response whatever to these pedagogical innovations, for they were not molded nor adequate to the specific diversities of their cultural characteristics, their racial conditions, their peculiar mentalities, nor to their miserable economic condition; and this last was the chief shortcoming. These pariahs needed, and needed badly, not alphabets and theoretic postulates but something which could show them the way to get enough to eat. Education, for this enormous majority of the Latin-American people, is inseparably linked with economic betterment, and to attempt this it would be necessary to reform completely not only machinery and organization but especially the existing criterion. One might almost have to start at the very beginning. For instance, it would be indispensable to take a true census, a true qualitative and quantitative evaluation of the inhabitants of Mexico, for those taken up to now have been done with slavish addiction to foreign methods. Consequently our population has been classified according to speech; and in the census published in 1918 by the

Department of Statistics, I3,143,372 persons are listed as Spanish-speaking and 1,690,356 as non-Spanish-speaking-that is, as Indians. The conclusions to be drawn would be that Mexico is composed of a great white, civilized majority and a small native, culturally backward minority. Laws, educational dispositions, political systems, etc., were established on such a statistical basis, tending therefore toward the exclusive betterment of the supposed white, Spanish-speaking modern majority, which is in reality a very small minority, for most of the inhabitants of Mexico are native, racially and culturally, though a large portion of them speak Spanish. This prolonged official error has left more than ten million Indians and halfbreeds entirely abandoned to their ignorant and miserable living, for the projects to help and educate them, supposing them white, always proved exotic and quite useless. The white minority, exclusively benefited by systems designed to help the total population, became more and more the directing, monopolizing and tyrannical element. In a study that I submitted to President Calles shortly before my connection with the Secretariat of Education, I suggested that, under the direction of a proposed Secretariat of Population, a thorough investigation be made of the true characteristics ⟦[[I33]⟧

and aspirations of the widely different social groups of which our people consist. Upon the basis of such knowledge as this, one could initiate an authoritative, parallel education for our masses, with a very definite tendency toward their economic betterment. The first thing would be to take a census in order to obtain the real number and value of the various components of our population. The numbers so procured would not be mere data with no practical use whatsoever, but would serve as nothing less than the foundation for new activities, for they would indicate very definitely through the information on the proportion of illiteracy, vital statistics, industrial poverty, racial and cultural conditions, etc., where help was most urgently needed. Keeping in mind precisely the integral character and ultimate use of this information, the census would be supplemented by information on the racial characteristics. This census would give various aspects and would therefore suggest orientations for a methodical, careful investigation of the Mexican people, their needs and shortcomings, with the practical end, already indicated, of ministering to the first and correcting the second. The preparatory data of the census would be a starting point for the scientific investigation of other phases of the life of the Mexican people:

vegetable, animal and mineral elements at the disposal of the inhabitants in each region, especially in Indian territories. These investigations, like the others, would not be of an exclusively scientific character but would have specifically utilitarian ends and tendencies, designed to localize, Identity, and develop the raw materials which, by means of simple and efficacious methods, the Indians could transform into easily negotiable industrial products and into products which would contribute to their own physical and cultural needs. At the same time the highly important relation of geography to human life should be studied. Generally speaking, to know the conditions under which a people lives it is indispensable to know those under which it developed in the past, for to a great extent, the present is to be explained by the past. This is especially true of a people such as the Mexican, formed of an indigenous majority which does not live on a modern plane of civilization but presents the same or a similar life to that during the Colonial period or even in pre-Historic times. Though a large part of our natives speak Spanish, their huts or jacales, their domestic utensils such as the metate (corn-grinder), the petate (leaf mat), the huarache (leather sandal), the haucal (crate for carrying produce), their pagan polytheism,

their ideas of witchcraft and magic, etc., are almost identically those of several centuries ago. The archaeological-historical evolution of our native population is therefore a necessary postulate to the true comprehension of its living conditions today. At present the white population of the country, smallest in number, develops under relatively satisfactory conditions, whereas the native and halfbreed generally suffer great moral and material wrongs, the origin of which lies in causes we should know but usually ignore, though their fatal effects could hardly be more patent: defective organic development, economic distress, illiteracy, isolation, retardation, etc.; and in view of this it seems logical to concentrate attention upon them. After obtaining some data on geographic resources and archaeological-historical antecedents, it would be of special interest to investigate carefully the actual anatomical, physiological, and pathological conditions of our natives, as well as their peculiar social organization; their economic situation; religious, moral, and artistic ideas; commercial, industrial, and cultural phenomena. Data that the census would give on density and distribution could be almost immediately applied for re-distribution wherever necessary or advisable.

Auto-colonization of the sparsely populated regions would at the same time improve the working conditions in the places inhabited by a fairly large number of laborers and farmers. Such colonies could be distributed for educational purposes in places where the people were most backward, and this would mean the first step toward the agricultural and industrial development of regions at present desert or badly cultivated, to which Mexicans might be sent from regions unfavorable to proper development, due to poverty of natural resources, excess population, etc. Upon the results of these investigations, which would without doubt give the true situation of our people, plans to normalize their development could be based. It is an exceedingly long task, and certain phases of it would prolong themselves indefinitely, so that it would be impossible to wait for its conclusion before beginning to educate the people. Parallel to investigation, therefore, education should begin to be implanted, always keeping in mind that any system adopted would not be related, except incidentally, to exclusively theoretic knowledge or pedagogy. The fundamental tendency in the education of our Mexican masses should, I think, be directed toward teaching them the best means of making a

living; how to develop and utilize the natural resources, fountains of life and well-being, which are so abundant in the cities and territories inhabited by them. In elaborating any system of education for Mexico, one should keep its geography well in mind, for, derived from the economic factor, prime in Mexican education is the topographic factor. The same things are not useful to everybody, and therefore, educationally Mexico falls into three geographic groups, and such studies as I have made of the problem, have been based on this fundamental classification: urban, rural, and coast region education. It is logical to suppose that we city dwellers know the sources of life and riches open to us. However, we do not. In the capital of Mexico, for instance, it would be hard to find any one person who could tell accurately and in detail the numerous and different ways by which a living might be made in the metropolis. The census and statistics should shed a good deal of light upon this aspect of city life, but unfortunately this information was not gathered with sufficient sociological perspective, and is therefore unsatisfactory. If it is true that the adults do not know what there is around them, it is obvious that the children

are even more ignorant in this respect. School teachers and parents are well acquainted with the vague outlook of a child at the end of his elementary, and sometimes even of his high-school, education. He does not know, he cannot choose, the field in which he can develop his capabilities, and this is the cause of many mistakes and failures and the beginning of far too many mediocre and passive lives. This deplorable situation is due to the eminently abstract character of the education which the child receives; and the passive attitude is a result of scholastic life, regulated by an abstract criterion. For example: Suppose that a Mexican youth, graduate of some elementary city school, needs to work for wages sufficient to live on, a position in which go per cent of the children of the Mexico City populace find themselves. This boy, who has some theoretic and superficial knowledge-reading, writing, arithmetic, geography-discovers the discouraging fact that he can find no productive use for his knowledge. It is insufficient in itself to justify a remunerative employment. Furthermore, this boy is ignorant of the thousand ways and means by which a city-wage is earned, he does not know where to find work, he is not acquainted with its nature and characteristics. He merely senses the enormous and chaotic honeycomb of the metropolis.

Finally, this boy does not possess a dynamically trained personality, but a passive one, molded in six years of confinement in his school. His vision is narrow and his curiosity as to what happens in the city—the true school, the school of real life-is dulled. After much drifting and many mistakes, this youth will find some sort of work, but rarely that wherein he could have used his faculties to best advantage. He might originally have had some inclination toward electricity and might have been a clever craftsman at it, or perhaps an active and enthusiastic clerk; but an abstract education and the very concrete necessity of making a living have driven him to be an illhumored chauffeur's apprentice or even a miserable newsboy. It might be pointed out that there are elementary schools in Mexico City which teach, in addition to the abstract subjects already mentioned, experimental gardening, agriculture, small crafts, and industries. I sincerely respect the good faith and the pioneer spirit of the organizers of these educational centers, but I do not think it justifiable to encourage them, for in the first place, it is illogical and anti-economical to suppose that city children will ever disdain a city-wage to go to the country and work as field hands at much smaller wages and

in an environment entirely different from that to which they are accustomed. In Mexico, as elsewhere, the exodus is from the country to the city, a thing to be deplored, and avoided if possible, but nevertheless a fact. I am not likely to be contradicted in my second objection, which is that the number of small crafts and industries taught-such as carpentry, blacksmithing, gardening, plumbing, baking, photography, dressmaking, embroidery, etc.—is infinitesimal compared to the actual number of crafts and industries which make up the web of a modern city such as the capital of Mexico, and with which the child should be acquainted in order to give his vocational awakening full opportunity. Finally, the small shops in which the pupils of such schools are taught are quite rudimentary, so that a child trained as a carpenter, blacksmith, or potter, is not equipped to work in factories which of course contain complex modern machinery, such as perforating saws, mechanical lathes, electric ovens, etc. The sphere of activity in these schools, no matter how good the instruction, is therefore limited; and the more so when the child is not made aware of the existence of other multiple urban activities which might yield him a livelihood. The solution of this particular problem is to be found in the preliminary investigation of the means

of livelihood which the city offers-the different ways of working, physically or intellectually, which are likely to yield either a daily wage or a monthly salary, or personal direct profit from the labor itself, forming with the information so obtained a progressive classification of activities, beginning with the most humble and going to the most complex. Upon such an investigation, a law could be projected which would obligate merchants, industrialists, constructors, and, in general, all employers according to the classification mentioned above to permit the school children to observe, at certain intervals and in detail, the working of their establishments. The factories and workshops of the nation should be automatically included in such a measure, heretofore untried in the city schools. After having been educated under a system with provisions such as these, the children would leave the schools knowing at least the ways of making a living in the city and how these are to be chosen to advantage, but most of all they will have had a chance to find out which of these holds the greatest attraction for them. If the economic factor is important in city education, it is even more so in rural; and its aspects

are, to a certain extent, similar. The sources of life to be found in the fields fall into two great groups: (1) agricultural products which directly (vegetable) or indirectly (animal) reward man's cultivation of the soil; (2) raw materials (animal, vegetable, or mineral) found in rural Mexico, which can be transformed into industrial objects for domestic use or for sale in national or foreign markets. The enormous area of our country and its small population, as well as the richness and profusion of raw materials at hand, might lead us to suppose that the rural inhabitants of Mexico live in a prosperous and enviable condition of physical and intellectual well-being. Quite the contrary, however, for the misery in which our great social majority lives is alarming, and its intellectual plane should be classed as primitive. This abnormal situation is due to the simple fact that the rural inhabitants have been confronted by great obstacles and have not known how to conquer them and therefore have not made satisfactory use of the natural resources within their grasp, to obtain from them the primary or secondary products which are the logical sources of life in whatever region they may live. In the first place, the uneven distribution of land ownership, and therefore of its products, has been the cause of grave economic problems, for the great

majority of rural inhabitants has never possessed lands nor utilized them directly, nor enjoyed their products, but has been subject to life within a very small compass. This situation is being altered slowly through establishment of a system of small land-owning. The second great obstacle which rural inhabitants encounter is a geographic, climatic one, for a large proportion of the land in our country, and especially that part owned by small proprietors, lacks irrigation and suffers the irregularities of the seasons, so that its yield is scanty or the crop a failure if it does not rain at the right time or the frosts are early. This situation could be relieved by the organizing of co-operative associations which would collectively construct dams, wells, and other channels for scientific irrigation. The third and chief difficulty in which the rural inhabitants find themselves is their own ignorance of the utilizable elements in their native territories, and of the means for making the necessary industrial transformation of those which they do know. Furthermore, even when they do own lands and waters, they generally cannot secure the corresponding benefit, for they have not the agricultural education necessary for the proper cultivation and selections of animal and plant breeds. Furthermore, because

they have always done so, they continue raising maize almost exclusively, and this, in spite of the fact that in many regions it is in reality the least profitable of crops. Education seems the answer to all these problems. Rural education should be more elemental and of shorter duration, so far as the purely scholastic end of it goes; whereas special attention should be given to agricultural and industrial teaching, so that the inhabitants may learn to take fullest advantage of those raw materials within their reach and to increase their crops, both in quantity and in quality. To impart rural education properly, the agricultural territories should be subdivided or classified according to geological formation, altitude, longitude, latitude, temperature, etc., and since the natural resources to be utilized vary greatly with these factors, the instruction about them should vary according to carefully mapped out zones. Another difficulty: how to distribute efficiently this theoretical agricultural-industrial education among millions of rural inhabitants? Where to find teachers for the thousands or tens of thousands of rural schools set apart for this labor of redemption and social reconstruction? The teachers trained in the national or state normal schools

would hardly be equipped for such a task, for teachers graduate from urban centers cannot possibly know, objectively and by experiment, the geographical, geological, agricultural, botanical, and zoölogical conditions of those regions to which they might later be sent; and they would therefore be unable to teach anything beyond the purely abstract knowledge which they themselves had received in the city, leaving their pupils still without instruction on how to cultivate and improve their lands and cattle, and how to effect the industrial and salable transformation of the natural elements available in each region. Further, no graduate of a national or state normal school would be willing to go to a rural school for a daily salary of from two to four pesos, which is a laborer's wage in the city. Socially, also, the teacher, molded to urban life, accustomed to city clothing, city food, lodging, and amusements, could hardly adapt himself satisfactorily to the rude life of a peasant; and, in the last analysis, he would be effecting his own retrogression by so doing.** The rural school teacher, the man destined to redeem for the peasant the burning and desert regions in the states of Coahuila and Nuevo Leon; = Because of these reasons, we believe that the creation of schools for Indian rural teachers at the metroplis or principal towns would be a failure.

the malarial and pest-ridden state territories of Guerrero, Oaxaca, Tabasco, Campeche, and Chiapas; the savage and scarcely peopled stretches of Durango, Lower California, Quintana Roo, etc., cannot be he who biologically, socially, and economically belongs to a metropolitan environment, with all its suave and artificial routine. Unquestionably this teacher must be a native of those regions, tempered to the burning suns of the lime plains or the sandy deserts; relatively immune to disease after innumerable generations of ancestors acclimated to the geographical and biological conditions. He should be accustomed to eating the tortilla and chili of the sierra, be acquainted with the mechanism of the plow, and should know how to sit on his horse. Educated in his native region, such a man is, potentially, the modern apostle of the rural school; for one sent from the city must inevitably prove a weak, anemic, exotic, and artificial transplantation. To procure such teachers, centers of education for them could be formed in the representative geographical, biological, and ethnographic zones already alluded to. "Centers of Cultural Incorporation" or rural normal schools could be established in each of these, where a hundred or more young men could be trained at a time, natives of the zone

to which the center belonged. The organization and respective duties of the students of such an institution would of course differ greatly from those of an ordinary normal school. In the first place, the teachers in these normal schools would be delegated by the Secretariats of Education, Agriculture, Industry, and Health for the following purposes: The Department of Education proper would provide teachers of theoretic and rudimentary subjects, and for the fostering of cultural life. The Secretariat of Industry would provide experts and foremen of industrial workshops, who would teach the identifying and localizing of prime vegetable, animal, or mineral elements, and the process of changing them into really useful objects for domestic use or for marketing. The Secretariat of Agriculture would send agricultural experts to teach the actual cultivation and breeding of regional plants and animals, using the central storehouse as the center of his action. The Department of Health would provide physicians whose duty would be to care for the health of the inhabitants and to teach them something of elemental hygiene and preventive medicine. The artistic gifts so vigorously manifest in the Mexican people should be further cultivated, for one aspect of which there could be set aside some

sort of place for a theater in which would be presented comedies, choruses, dances, lectures, moving pictures, radio concerts, etc., such a theater being, wherever practicable, an open-air structure. Besides the necessary provision for the teacherdelegates, there would be dormitories, diningrooms, and baths for the pupils; and these pupils, future teachers, would be chosen from among the most promising of the native youths of each zone containing a school or center. They would be youths not under eighteen nor over twenty-two. In my previous studies on this problem of rural education in Mexico, I have always included the mention of some provision for the woman, for it is a clearly observable fact that the native Mexican woman is in almost the same condition of servitude as in the past. The centers indicated above would therefore not only educate professors but also women teachers, by a faculty of women competent and interested in the task. ' After one or two years in this school, the teachers could be sent out into the rural districts upon a small salary comparable to that which other workers would expect to receive in their native regions. One must of course not forget that, given the cultural equipment of these teachers, they would not impart a high degree of instruction in the

rural schools. But if they succeeded in teaching the peasants the true biological and social needs of a normal human life, if they managed to decrease the large percentage of illiteracy, if they could make them see how to wrest a proper living from the natural sources all around them, they would be doing what for over a century has been proclaimed—redeeming the Mexican masses—a proclamation which has not heretofore gone beyond the idle phrases of an inconscient and vain attitude. One of the most serious, and not generally recognized, obstacles in the path of the normal development of our people is their under-nourishment; this is the fundamental cause of the exaggerated rates of mortality and the relative lack of dynamic impulse which can be observed in their activities. We have already referred to the many ways of living open to both urban and rural inhabitants. Especially interesting are the organic resources of the coast regions, and the industries derived therefrom. We shall not discuss here the dietetic value of fish, it being enough to state that it is almost equal to beef and that it is the basic food for hundreds of millions of men all over the world and a

source of wealth in many countries, even in some whose coasts are not very extensive. For example, there are the British Isles, whose statistics on the fishing industry for the year I905, before the use of the motor-boat, now considered almost indispensable, are especially worthy of attention. The fishing industry for that year netted Great Britain over 100,000,000 pesos and gave employment to 110,000 people. The treasury spent only $312,000 in the administration of the national fisheries and $148,000 in scientifically fostering the development of this industry. To such figures Mexico presents a dismaying contrast. Our coasts are exaggeratedly extensive 9,000 kilometers. Along them can be found a great variety and number of species, especially those that fall into the three usual classifications: coast fish and sea food, shallow water open-sea fish, and deep water open-sea fish. Our coast population has all the ability and the necessary daring of any seagoing people. These antecedents would lead one to expect at least that fish or sea food would occupy a fairly important place on our menu, since it might be considered too much to expect its exportation. Instead, one finds that fresh fish is a rich man's dish, and this in season only; salt and canned fish is imported from foreign countries and never comes

from our own coasts, and it is of course sold at prices way beyond the average reach. The defective means of transportation from coast to interior explain this disastrous situation to a great extent, but there is another and more fundamental cause. We do not know the modern and efficient methods of the industry; we do not know how to fish, how to preserve the fish either in cans or salt, and we do not properly pack that which is consumed fresh. We make no use at all of the potential riches derived from the industry, such as tortoise-shell, pearl, coral, mother of pearl, or sea vegetable products. We have not even attempted to create markets for coast products in the interior of the country, let alone export them. In a word, we do not know how to make practical use of the inexhaustible possibilities in 9,000 kilometers of coast whose only limit is the open sea. Here, again, the problem is educational, and its solution consists merely in teaching the coast population the most practical and efficient means of obtaining the maximum production from sea sources. When this has been procured, our national alimentation will have been bettered at least I00 per cent, and this would of course mean the satisfactory organic development of our people and greater profits on its labors. The now flourishing

physical and economic development of England, Sweden, Norway, Japan, and other fish-eating peoples should seem ample foundation for our optimism in this respect. The logical course of action would be to select several coast zones, representative of our littoral regions, and to establish in them educational centers which, besides giving the theoretic knowledge which is equally valuable in city, field, or coast, would teach the coast inhabitants the most modern and efficient fishery methods, in which particular instruction the Secretariat of Agriculture should collaborate, and in which the Secretariat of Industry might profitably assist in teaching the best industrial use of sea products. The Department of Health should in its turn send specialists effectively to fight the malarial fever, that terrible coast plague, and to introduce hygienic and preventive habits. The Secretariat of Industry and Commerce should then localize markets for sea products and make their transportation easier. The Secretariat of Finance (Hacienda) should help by projecting fiscal means of protecting and encouraging new and old sea industries. Finally, the projected Secretariat of Population would co-ordinate and make effective the studies and conclusions at which it might have arrived.

I have had the honor of collaborating in some of the educational experiments which have been made in Mexico, and these conclusions are the result of my investigations. Above all, I would repeat the importance of the economic factor in Mexican education as a fundamental in the success or failure of whatever project is undertaken, and derived from this factor, the geographical one. For Mexico, as I have often said, is a heterogeneous country and should have its own special and peculiar system adapted to its many different needs, which can be gauged scientifically. Educationally, one must minister to each element as each element demands, in order to effect, paradoxically enough, a real unity, by lifting them all to the same plane of civilization. And by civilization I do not mean merely teaching the Indian how to read. I mean teaching him that he walks on rich soil and that there is a world around him. Throughout four hundred years he has stagnated miserably and has not even known it. He has not seen the failure of his efforts. He thinks he leads a normal existence; education will make him see that he can lead a better one and how he can do so.

TIONS BETWEEN THE UNITED Of as much or more interest to the American people than European or Asiatic politics, is the Mexican situation. Indeed, Mexico is a faithful mirror of the international aspirations and social needs of nearly all the countries from the Rio Grande to the Straits of Magellan, and as such it is valuable to the United States. It is also the very sensitive thermometer which registers to a degree the surges which successively warm and cool the attitude of the southern countries toward the United States. Finally, Mexico promises the brightest future to American industry, for it is now undergoing a most interesting economic-social change, which is an increase in the number of consumers of modern merchandise from three or four million to fifteen million. By raising the level of mass culture, chiefly of the Indians, their physical and mental wants, at present quite elemental and primitive, are automatically multiplied and intensified. The same holds true for the rest of Latin America.

The approximate twenty or thirty million consumers will in the near future become one hundred million. They will be people who have acquired and developed the demand for modern life and comfort, if the means to achieve such an end are opportunely taken. What country would be likely to benefit by this new enormous market? Certainly that producer-nation which possesses or has gained not only the good will of the respective Latin-American governments but, what is far more important, a foreseeing and ample comprehension of the needs, aspirations, and tendencies of those future buyers. It must be kept in mind that the Mexicans are the continerital touchstone. So much for the economic side of the matter. As for the spiritual, sentimental, social, or any other, point of view, such understanding is even more vital. Let us consider, for example, the entirely different attitudes of Americans toward Mexicans and toward Canadians. The American esteems the Canadian, not only because cordial diplomatic and economic bonds unite the two governments, but also because the Canadian is of the same race, speech, and culture. The American accepts the Canadian on his own mental footing. On the other hand, he ignores or despises the Mexican, of whom he often has a distorted or vague idea; a

circumstance due partly to the fact that the majority of the Mexicans who go to the United States are uncultured emigrants, competitors of American labor, seen only in their coarse industrial aspects. It is about time for the American people to begin to acquire that accurate comprehension of Mexico which they lack in spite of the fact that, since the fall of the Diaz government some fifteen years ago, Mexico has been a pet topic of the American press. Much of the public ignorance is to be blamed on deliberately biased and malicious press reports sent out by unconditional and persistent enemies of Mexico, whose standards are fixed and whose paths are determined by uncontrolled prejudices and passions. They usually succeed in placing Mexico before the United States in a most unflattering light. On the other hand, the friends of the country, whether generous and unselfish or paid to do so, write of Mexico as a veritable promised land, a paradise of delicious fruits and rich metals and marvelous scenery. They picture Mexicans as simple and amiable creatures among whom the foreigner leads a comfortable and gently happy life. Of course not everything written about Mexico falls into one of these two classes. There have been accurate and sane reports, but at exceedingly rare intervals. There have existed, and

do exist, irreproachable sources of information upon several aspects of Mexican life; these are the studies and investigations made by American scientists. Unfortunately, these studies, of interest to a limited number of specialists, hardly ever reach the general public-the man on the street. Upon no more foundation than contradictory, deficient, and exaggerated reports, the American people can hardly be expected to form a satisfactory, just opinion of the complicated Mexican-American problem. I have asked American people chosen as types from different social strata for judgment on the relations between Mexico and the United States; and the average answer, to me the most interesting, was briefly this: The American people and the Mexicans are two groups of human beings living under liberal and democratic laws in two countries exceptionally rich in natural resources. Yet the wellbeing of Americans of all classes is generally far superior to the corresponding situation of Mexicans. The United States has had only one civil war throughout its hundred and fifty years of independence, while Mexico and her sister republics have nearly all suffered incessant revolutions and the corresponding hardships during one hundred years of independence. It is hard to account for this difference between the lives of two peoples when conditions fundamental for development seem to have been identically favorable to both. For fifteen years, at least, the relations between Mexico and the United States have been unstable, hostile, and dangerous in spite of the fact

that the two countries have many things in common and should be on the harmonious and satisfactory terms that their geographic positions and mutual economic advantage demand. With the parallel here logically established, as a starting point to prove that the relations between Mexico and the United States are faulty, I shall make several observations, always with the understanding that I accept and appreciate such corrections as may be suggested. Our international relations cannot be bettered effectively and permanently without giving proper attention to several considerations: (I) The Mexican people have been living under very bad conditions from time immemorial, and these must be improved. The natural resources in Mexico are practically virgin, and some development and utilization of them must be begun, for it is both antibiological and anti-social to expect a strong and rich people to be the cordial and friendly neighbor of a poor and weak one. (2) The American people ought to realize that if the Mexicans have not satisfactorily utilized the riches of their country and have lived in disastrous revolution and suffered great economic hardships, all of which has reflected unfavorably upon foreign investment, it has not been because of a temperamental and anti-cosmic

idea of self-annihilation but because grave geographical, biological, historical, and racial obstacles have appeared constantly in the path of Mexican progress, often blocking it completely. The American people have had few if any difficulties to face when compared with the many and serious problems which have beset Mexico. These fundamental inequalities explain also the relative ease in governing the United States, compared to the same problem in Mexico. (3) American capital is less interested in the losses foreign investment suffered during past revolutions in Mexico, than in the future possibilities the country has to offer— future investments of the surplus billions which create annoying financial competition in the United States. It will not be long before gigantic investments will be made in Mexico; and they will be made as they are in the United States, that is, by making the same or similar concessions to the economic well-being of the country or community, though in Mexico, even with these concessions, the investment is likely to prove far more profitable. (4) The old idea of diplomacy based exclusively on economic advantage is losing prestige. In the near future, all diplomacy will be based on strictly scientific principles. Legations and embassies will function almost as official annexes of a university. by

They will investigate the cultural, psychical, racial, and social aspects of the countries wherein they are stationed; and this will bring about, among other things, closer and more productive, more just and humane international relations, at present unfortunately still established and swayed exclusively by economic motives. The best proof the United States could give of its Pan-Americanism would be to initiate just such diplomacy in Latin America. Let us make a brief geographical analysis of the United States and Mexico. It is often said that nature is wise and generous, for it supplies amply all human needs. The United States should, indeed, be deeply grateful to her; for besides making of its territory a rich and abundant natural warehouse, she bestowed upon it the facilities for taking effective advantage of its treasures. With Mexico, the loving Mother was equally lavish in the matter of initial boons, but perversely made the development of the potential resources quite difficult. The first obstacle to human enterprise in Mexico is topography itself, that is, the lay of the land is exaggeratedly accidental. Mountains are numerous and plains scarce. This is not entirely a disadvantage. It means in certain instances a greater possibility of generating hydro-electric energy; it means a larger field of exposed mineral veins and

strata; but it also means great difficulty of transportation of people and products from one region to another, and also many complications in agricultural development. In the United States, natural and manufactured products can be transported fairly easily and cheaply from camp and factory to consumer by rail. In Mexico there are thousands and thousands of square miles covered with cedar, mahogany, and sandalwood forests, but these precious woods cannot be lumbered because they are surrounded by rivers, mountains, and cliffs, and constructing railroads to these forests would mean multiplying the actual cost four or five times, due to the number of cuts, bridges, and tunnels that would be needed. Certain special hats, made of palm leaves and bought by the millions in the Southern United States, come from a mountainous region whose borders touch the states of Pueblo and Oaxaca; and the only route to it is a trail so complicated by topographical accidents that the hats have to be carried by Indians in packs, for often not even horses or mules can thread their way along the rough trails in the sierra. The palm hat industry is a very important one, but even so, it could never justify nor compensate for the construction of a railroad in such a mountainous region. The relatively few railroads

which in the United States cross difficult country are considered works of art and are advertised profusely to the tourist. In this respect, Mexico could well be considered an enormous art gallery, for nearly all of its railroads are literally sculptured in the sierras. Due to the numerous and complicated mountain ranges in Mexican territory, waterways are deficient. There are five or six rivers which might be termed navigable; the rest are swift and dangerous torrents which during the rainy season carry the water on the high table lands to the sea and which in the dry season are scarcely streams. Therefore, transportation by water is hardly plausible; whereas, in the United States the proportion of flat to rocky country is incomparably greater than in Mexico, and navigable rivers are numerous. Cotton, tobacco, cattle, and other products can be sent from the south and west to the north and east by railroads whose initial cost has been normal, or by rivers which were the gracious and spontaneous gifts of Mother Nature. The coal and machinery produced in northern and eastern mines and factories can be sent back by the same routes. As to agriculture, Mexico again encounters difficulties due to the exaggerated mountainous nature of the land. Most of the water runs quickly from

slope to slope down to the narrow belts of land which form the coasts, or to the few closed or semiclosed valleys like the valleys of Mexico, Oaxaca, and Cuernavaca, etc. This circumstance, added to the irregularity of rain and the frequent early frosts, explains Mexico's small crop in relation to its area and the average quality of its land. Tradition sings the praises of the fertile Mexican tropics, but in reality their merits have been much exaggerated. Though the land is very rich, the unhealthy climate is so destructive of human life that, in the last analysis and according to statistics, production is mediocre. Until radical cures are found for tropical diseases, most of all. for malaria, it may be stated that agricultural production in the Mexican tropics and in the southern countries, where conditions are analogous, will not reach even normal, and many lives will still be lost. One more, and most important, factor must be considered in Mexican agriculture. The variety of temperatures, due principally to the often-cited mountainous structure, makes that generalization or standardization essential to cultivation impossible. In the states of Puebla, Oaxaca, Chiapas, Michoacán, Jalisco, and many others the same soil produces sugar cane and wheat—that is, tropical products and cold-country vegetation are found

together. Botanically, it seems logical that wheat, barley, potatoes, and other plants should develop to better advantage in cold countries which are suited to their growth; whereas sugar cane, coffee, etc., would naturally grow better in those tropical regions where they originated. It would be valuable to investigate what plants really flourish in those mixed climates and which should be transplanted to other territories. The only notable standardized regions in the general heterogeneity are Yucatan and the Laguna cotton country in Northern Mexico. Given the dry climate, the lime-shot soil, and the warm temperature of Yucatan, it can be seen how, after long and careful experiment, the hennequen or sisal, of which ropes and cables are made, was established as its most productive crop. Immediately, all other domestic vegetation was substituted by hennequen to such an extent that now Yucatan has to import even the most elemental necessities, such as industrial tools, cereal foods, and cattle. But on the other hand, this state produces more hennequen than any other place in the world, and it is literally criss-crossed with railroads; while its people live under much better conditions than those of the other states in the republic. A parallel, though less characteristic situation exists in the Laguna cotton

zone. In the United States, however, geographical conditions make standardized zones not only possible but the general rule instead of the exception. This means abundant and economical production. Thus there are the classic corn, cotton, wheat, and cattle belts. From the point of view of political geography, one might make jocose, but justified, comment. The extensive plains and prairies of Argentina and North America-the wide horizons, the regular, monotonous surfaces—seem to create a spirit of tranquillity, of peaceful, anti-revolutionary content in the inhabitants; while the symbolic aspect of Mexican territory seems to be reflected in its people, whose lives parallel the conflict of mountains, the protest of fiery volcanoes, the sudden, violent torrents which tear trees from their roots and destroy entire villages. The very land is geologically both very new and very old, battling continually to secure place and equilibrium. Such broken country means secure shelter in every square yard of it for a wild animal or a bandit. That is why, traditionally, Mexico has always been pestered by one or more bands of political malcontents or out-and-out bandits who, in their mountain or forest retreats, are safe from all attack; an eloquent example is provided by the case

of Pancho Villa, who although surrounded by General Pershing's men and wounded in the leg was saved by a good hiding place in a canyon. It will be argued, perhaps, that there are countries where, in spite of geographical difficulties and even with scant natural resources, agricultural production is large, due to the fact that the energy, competence, and traditional training of their people have been sufficient to overcome the obstacles nature has imposed. Such an argument would mean ignorance of the fact that the aboriginal Mexicans were an energetic race of tenacious and often victorious warriors with nature. When the first indigenous immigrants came to Mexico, all vegetation was wild; and they did not even know which was nutritive and which poisonous. Through the centuries, the Indian made his terrible experiment at the cost of his life; and, thanks to this labor, corn, which was a wild grass, is a cereal which at present feeds a large part of humanity. The tomato, without which no American luncheon table is complete, is also an Indian contribution, as is chocolate, justly called a beverage of the gods. He also discovered and began to utilize many minerals. The Mexican of our day is by no means idle. He is attempting to change the difficult geographical conditions of « Euchleana Mexicana.

his country into favorable ones, as is demonstrated by the irrigation projects now being carried out on a large scale, and the railways and automobile highways also under construction. To resume the above analysis, it can be said that although Mexico possesses natural resources which are, in proportion to its area and its population, as rich and abundant as those of the United States and even richer, especially in the tropics, it does not have the geographical facilities which in the United States make the development of those resources a fairly easy and effective matter. The real American people, generous and idealistic, are not consciously hostile to the Mexican. They are merely ignorant of his antecedents, his social characteristics, his economic needs, and his spiritual tendencies. The reply might be that the Mexicans are likewise ignorant of American problems, which is in fact absolutely true. Let us glance rapidly over both aspects of the situation. Until a very tew years ago we were not only unacquainted with the conditions of natural and international development of the United States and the real value of Mexican-American harmonious relations, but we did not even know why we were hindered in our own evolution, what were the

fundamental causes of our retardation. A historical synthesis, however, will reveal them. From the arrival of Cortes, the Spanish conquerors had no other object in their legislation and organization than the substitution of their language, customs, and civilization for that of the natives, but they failed because the Indians defended themselves; first with arms, and then, conquered physically, by a passive resistance which has outlasted three centuries. When Mexican independence was declared, the great mass of natives and half-breeds which formed the majority of the population were at an economic and cultural level below the pre-Hispanic standards, for they had been rifled of their national resources, and the most brilliant phases of their culture had been erased; while they themselves had refused to accept the civilization of the conquerors. They were left without either, in utter wretchedness and with a defective hybrid culture which has characterized them ever since. In view of this unfortunate colonial experience, the now acclimated white minority, which controlled the country, should have once more initiated a harmonious fusion between itself and the • helpless majority, making and interpreting laws

which would satisfy the economic and social necessities of both groups; but instead of this, proceeding with a foreign and egoistic criterion, it precipitately collected the legal and constitutional precepts of foreign peoples, mixed them with the already existing ones of Hispanic origin, and presented them to the country as a monument of wisdom and patriotism. The situation of the native masses became still more difficult and miserable than in the Colonial period, for at least then there had existed, though hardly more than nominally, the somewhat palliative "Laws of Indies." It is because of this that the revolutions of the nineteenth century and early twentieth have been so much more numerous and intense than those of the three preceding centuries. At bottom, this dismal situation was caused by the absolute lack of knowledge on the part of the Mexican government of the real social structure of its people, since some of them believed in all good faith that to establish the ultra-modern laws of other peoples, even though the latter were ethnically, socially, and culturally different, was sufficient to produce its well-being. What more could they want? Thus we lived until the fall of General Diaz. It would therefore be illogical indeed to expect us to be familiar with the problems of the United States when we

Finally, such interest arose in Mexico in the study and understanding of its people that by order of the present executive, Plutarco Elias Calles, it was proposed that a Secretariat of Population be organized, which would be scientifically organized and adapted to our social, racial, and economic medium—a project which signifies one of the most original and transcendent achievements of any modern government, for it means the direct participation of scientific opinion in the government of a people. Returning to the question of our knowledge of the United States, it can be asserted that we really are entirely ignorant of the great qualities of the American people, since what we were accustomed to observe in the few Americans who were in direct contact with our country was by no means an indication of the nature of all the rest. The fact is that those few were, in the first place, the American diplomatic representatives who generally had high political positions in the United States or belonged to the aristocratic class but who neither knew our social characteristics and racial prejudices nor what course our ideals and tendencies were taking or might be expected to take. The re- Digitiżed by '

ports that these representatives sent to the Department of State, and to which Congress referred for information about Mexico, were for many years flattering and rosy, which was perfectly natural since they proceeded from three beings harmoniously united and allied into a single Trinity: President Diaz and his executive body, the conservative minorities and clergy, and the industrial and commercial cliques. To American representatives our nation meant nothing more than this triple alliance; and if it were kept content, northern diplomacy had nothing more to wish for. They knew nothing of the middle classes, which in Mexico, as everywhere, are the brain of the nation; nor of the humble people, who are its arms and hands. At the most, they had seen the picturesque Indian dances in the suburban Villa de Guadalupe on the twelfth of December, and with their tourist countrymen had been more or less agreeably amazed and startled. The disease, misery, slavery, and agony of those humble classes were drowned in the noise of the cosmopolitan capital. There were, nevertheless, Americans closely aware of the social problems then vital; and they could have advised their embassy that the horrible living conditions of the greater part of the people, and especially of the Indians, would sooner or later [ 1742]

mean a movement for liberation and social betterment. These men, who could have been excellent outposts of the embassy and even of the Department of State, were, however, scientists sent altruistically and for no gain by American universities and scientific institutions. Unfortunately, such conclusions as they arrived at appeared to be of no interest whatsoever to American diplomats; for, frankly, these investigators were always snubbed. That is, as far as the embassy was concerned, these men were given the consideration due American citizens; but their scientific point of view, formed after thoroughly investigating the social, psychic, or ethnic problems of the Mexican people, meant nothing at all to those diplomats of the old school, laboring under the dead weight of tradition. One might question the many American scientists who disinterestedly came to study Mexico and her problems in those days, might ask them whether their opinions were ever taken into consideration, and one would be convinced that, with very rare exceptions, never or hardly ever were they listened to. Purely dynamic causes had already brought a long-accumulated social discontent to the point where revolution might break out upon any pretext. The torch was applied by Madero, curiously

enough a member of the wealthy and ruling minority, a man whose soul was moved to pity by the sufferings of the people. Since Madero did not belong either to the middle or lower classes, his revolution became, surrounded as it was by difficulties, hardly more than a superficial movement. The embers of economic injustice and social discontent did not blaze up until later. Logically and inevitably, then, arose Carranza, Obregón, Calles, and men of their stamp, who razed the old institutions to the ground to build an entirely new social edifice in place of these anachronisms. One cannot insist that this transformation is perfect, and one must admit that in its course it has suffered unnecessary evils and gone to reactionary extremes; but even these things have been the natural consequences of natural causes, and any people, emerging from a state similar to that in which we were, would have gone by the same route. Let us examine closely the policies of American diplomacy during the long period of revolution. When Madero became president, the American representative was surprised by this dissolution of the trinity which had heretofore meant "Mexico" to the diplomatic corps, for though the martyr president had belonged to the conservative minority

by caste, his comrades in revolution had torn him away from this class and most of its ideals and wanted to make him completely like themselves. When President Madero was assassinated, the American diplomat informed Washington that the nation, to him still represented by the driftwood of the well-known trinity, was discontented under President Madero and had therefore sacrificed him to substitute some other executive. The American executive, however, sensed that somewhere the voice of the people, the middle and lower classes, had been muffled; and later investigation corroborated him, for it disclosed that the great and democratic Mexican majority loved Madero, who had been brought down by the conservative minorities and other elements, with foreign aid. Washington wavered, recognizing that here there was a real cause, and this cause, after bloody and bitter struggle, triumphed. During the government of Carranza the American representative had to reconcile the old and hostile criterion, based on the definitely past traditional trinity, with the new order of things. Carranza, a man of many faults but withal a true progressive and a man of the people, wanted the United States to understand as far as possible the justice of his people's demands; while the conservative

minorities we have mentioned, the business men and the foreigners, played to make the representatives listen only to their own need and desires. Therefore, in spite of the evident good intention at Washington to arrive at a fair and democratic appreciation of our citation, the embassy's point of view prevailed; and this point of view was identical with that of the conservatives and reactionaries, though its effect was often fought and even nullified by the personal effort of President Wilson. During the Obregón Administration, Ambassador Warren took a neutral and broad-minded stand; for, while he listened to the opinions of the conservatives and of the foreign business men, he also abandoned all diplomatic tradition and informed himself, as much as was within his power, upon the conditions and necessities of the social majorities, especially in their relation to international affairs, going for his information directly to original sources. Of Ambassador Sheffield in his official capacity I know little, having been away from my country for over a year and being consequently somewhat out of touch with its diplomatic life. But to return to our original theme, the Mexican government, throughout these last years, not satisfied with knowing the American people only

through its diplomatic representatives and its business men, has sought and obtained more intimate relations. Broad-minded and unscheming scientists, artists, labor leaders, and newspaper men have been attracted to the country. Every year a number of Mexican youths are sent to the United States to school to study and understand the ideas and ideals of their colleagues. At the same time it has been made easy and attractive for American students to come to the Mexican National University, especially to the now famous summer sessions. From the purely diplomatic point of view, Mexico has initiated a new policy in the United States and other countries, an excellent illustration of which is the present Mexican ambassador to Washington, who does not owe his position to political virtues, for he has always been outside of politics, and who furthermore has never given exclusive importance to the canons of traditional diplomacy. He is undoubtedly the first ambassador to really represent the Mexican people in the United States, and not merely the aristocrats and plutocrats, as most all his predecessors have done. He has ample perspective and integral knowledge of the social structure of our country; of its characteristics and tendencies; above all, wherein these concern or touch the United States. Furthermore,

he is well aware of the social, economic, and political problems of the American people and can therefore always know when any of them affect Mexico, directly or indirectly. Finally, for some time there has existed in Mexican legations and embassies an attaché who represents exclusively the middle and lower classes and whose task it is to investigate the best means employed elsewhere to better the living conditions of those classes. This is what Mexico has done to know the American people and make them know us. What, concretely, has been the corresponding work of the United States of America? There are two phases to this subject: (I) the official judgments of the American government upon Mexico, and the sphere to which these have been limited; (2) the knowledge which unofficial American individuals or institutions may have of Mexico, and the circle in which this information has been distributed. In the first place, Mexico, a country eminently rich in natural resources and raw materials, whose industrial production is of little importance, has always been considered the closest and most logical customer of American industries, and furthermore the most convenient and economical market for raw materials of the same industries. Also, Mexico

has been the field for investing billions of dollars to make them produce more than they would in the United States. Upon such antecedents have our diplomatic relations been based. The American embassies have generally functioned only as agents of great international business. There never was any social contact, any sympathy of spirit, any altruism or human co-operation between the two; and therefore, even from a purely commercial point of view, this exchange was always bad or at best mediocre. In Mexico, we repeat, there are four million buyers and sellers, whose business with the United States reaches an annual figure of 400,000,000 pesos; but there are also those other ten or twelve million who could also buy and sell approximately I,500,000,000 pesos annually, but who do not because, first of all, American business men have not attempted, privately or officially, to transform these millions of passive neighbors into active customers or salesmen. Relatively and in proportion, Wanamaker and Gimbel and merchants of their type, by sacrificing a few millions of profit, achieve a greater success and corresponding profit. They provide for the needs of their customers; and besides the exquisite courtesy and service, they have moderately priced restaurants, first-aid booths,

restrooms, washrooms, telephone and telegraph service, etc. International business is far from this goal. American interests have hardly ever willingly ceded some part of their profits for the economic and social betterment of the millions of Mexicans, who, as we have already said, could, if incorporated into even an elementary civilization, mean a new market and an increase of 400 per cent in the commercial balance between the two nations. The system followed has been solely that bad business policy of continual coolness and friction, not taking into consideration at all that most important of factors, the human factor, and the only one which means smooth, flexible, well-lubricated international relations. Most significant of all is the fact that the only reason for this policy is official custom and tradition. Non-official investigations have been conducted by American institutions whose tendency is altruistic and disinterested. They have gained a knowledge of the human aspects of Mexican problems, and their influence could be of great value in effectively bettering the diplomatic relations between the two countries; so also could the Pan-American Union, more than anything a potential institution, whose work could be of as great value

as that of the several expeditions and investigators idealistically working in the Mexican field. The Rockefeller Foundation has collaborated with several Mexican administrations in the most noble task possible-that of saving thousands and millions of potential victims from the yellow fever. The American Geographic Society, in its very important book The Land Problems of México by McBride, demonstrates objectively and scientifically that to better the economic conditions of the Mexican people it is fundamentally necessary to create small property, a conclusion which justifies the Mexican land and property laws, the spirit of which has been much misunderstood. The Carnegie Institute intelligently investigates just what factors made the Maya race of Yucatan, one of the most civilized in the world; and we Mexicans now face the task of investigating just what factors brought about its present-day decadence and what means would lift it to civilization on a modern plane. The Brookings School of Economics and Government has sent to Mexico intelligent investigators of economic relations between the two countries. The Social Science Research Council of Chicago is about to begin, with the collaboration of Mexicans,

an investigation of a transcendent problem, that of Mexican immigration • into the United States. Finally, the Norman Wait Harris Memorial Foundation of the great University of Chicago has organized and is carrying out one of the most interesting projects which have been undertaken with reference to Mexican-American problems. The list of institutions and persons who labor at this great task of achieving harmonious and fraternal relations between the United States and Mexico is a long one. The key to the situation is the material progress of Mexico, and direct or indirect co-operation toward this end is a definite and objective means of eliminating our eternal apple of discord—the economic differences between the two nations. Unfortunately, the results of this noble and highly important work reach a limited circle and play a passive rôle in the official relations of American administrations toward Mexico. This fact is easily explained, for these generous and cultured institutions labor alone, privately, and the results of their investigations are generally one-sided though of high value as such. In view of these circumstances and moved not only by scientific interest, but also and chiefly by

that interest which my country arouses in me, I permit myself, in conclusion, to suggest: Let the many scientific institutions I have already named each choose a specialist, these specialists to form a great advisory body dedicated to the integration and compilation of the data procured by those institutions individually, in reference to Latin-American problems as related to the United States, beginning with the Mexicans since they are the most representative of the southern countries. Then, let the synthesis and conclusions reached in that work be published and circulated profusely through all the United States and all its social organizations. These disinterested studies and investigations which have been made about Mexico, chiefly those on social sciences, would be of value to the Department of State at Washington, were the serene and impartial opinions contained therein allowed some part in forming a justified policy toward the southern countries. Further, since all American embassies and legations in our countries have a military attaché who studies problems pertaining to his science, and a commercial attaché whose duty it is to foster and aid purely material interchange, why not send also a scientific attaché to investigate that most interesting factor in international relations, the human factor; and thereby discover the reason

for the social and cultural hostility between the Anglo-Saxon and Indo-Hispanic elements on this continent, and propose the remedy for such a situation. When such a corps of representatives from all the intellectual institutions of the United States can show to the Department of State the conclusions at which it has been able to arrive, it is probable that these conclusions would begin to have some weight and influence in the American policy toward Latin-American countries. If these conclusions can be made to reach the American people, in popular printed form, a true approach and true unification of ideals shall have been begun for the people of this continent.
